articles.title: Motorola details everything coming with its big Android 17 update
articles.author: sanujb6@gmail.com (Sanuj Bhatia) , Sanuj Bhatia
articles.content:
What you need to know
- Motorola has detailed the new features coming to its phones with the upcoming Android 17 software update.
- Android 17 will bring stackable widgets, themed icons, Live Updates, and AI-powered notification summaries.
- More than 50 Motorola phones are confirmed to receive Android 17, including recent Razr and Edge models.
We finally know what features Motorola is bringing to its phones with the Android 17 update.
Now that Google has rolled out Android 17 for Pixel phones, more brands are starting to detail their own updates. We recently saw Nothing showcase Nothing OS 5.0 based on Android 17, and now Motorola has revealed some of the features coming to its devices.
As detailed on Motorola India's support page, the Android 17 update will bring changes to the home screen and notifications, alongside several new security features. One of the biggest additions is stackable widgets, which will let users combine multiple widgets into a single block on the home screen. Users will also be able to use themed icons and hide labels from Quick Settings tiles.
In terms of notifications, Motorola is finally adding support for Live Updates, alongside notification summaries that can condense longer notifications into a single sentence for quicker reading.
Motorola also says eligible devices will use machine learning models to identify low-priority notifications and bundle them into a separate quiet section under silent notifications.
You can check out Motorola's full Android 17 changelog below:
Home screen and quick settings improvements
Stackable widgets
You can now stack widgets, combining multiple widgets into a single block on your home screen. Instead of taking up several grids on your home screen for your weather, calendar, battery and music player, stack them and swipe the stack to switch between them.
Themed icons
You can now use an icon theme that coordinates with your overall theme. Touch & hold a blank space on your Home screen, then tap Home settings > Themed icons.
Hide quick setting labels when using Classic style
If you're using Classic style for quick settings, you can now hide labels on the settings tiles. Hiding them frees up screen space if you already recognise the icons.
Improved notifications
Live updates
Live updates let apps to display real-time, ongoing data. Instead of sending multiple notifications, an app can now continuously update a single live snippet in your status bar or notifications. You can turn these on or off.
Notification summaries
You can now peek at your notifications for a one-sentence summary of a lengthy group chat or a rapid-fire thread from messaging apps (like WhatsApp or Messages).
Organised notifications
Your phone now organises your notifications to separate your personal messages from clutter and automated alerts. It uses machine learning to screen lower-priority notifications and bundles them into separate, quiet folders under the Silent section of your notifications.
New settings
Enhanced HDR brightness control
When you view HDR content – like an Ultra HDR photo in Google Photos, a HDR video on YouTube or an HDR feed on Instagram – your phone's display automatically sets brightness to its highest limits to make the highlights pop.
You can now limit this brightness to a more comfortable level by adjusting the intensity of Enhanced HDR brightness or turning it off to force HDR photos and videos to play at a normal brightness level.
New sharing features in Connected devices
There are two new ways to share in Settings > Connected devices:
To share a photo or file with one other person, use Tap to Share by placing your phones together. To share with a reusable group, use Quick Drop to send photos or files to friends or a team simultaneously.
Other improvements
Android system upgrades add more than new features. Using the latest Android update provides other improvements such as:
Enhanced security and protection to defend against evolving threats like malware, phishing and data breaches.
App compatibility with newer apps, which often require the latest Android version to function correctly.
Performance improvements that optimise your phone's operating system for smoother performance, better stability and, in some cases, longer battery life.
Bug fixes and stability enhancements to resolve known issues and improve overall reliability and stability
There are a few other changes coming as well. As highlighted in a report by FoneArena, Motorola's Android 17 update will bring improvements to cross-platform Quick Share, although that still doesn't include AirDrop compatibility with iPhones. You can also expect features like Audio Sharing, a refreshed Quick Settings panel, and improved HDR brightness management.
Motorola has already confirmed that Android 17 will roll out to more than 50 devices, including several recent Razr and Edge models. You can check out the full list of Motorola phones getting Android 17 right here.
Sanuj is a tech writer who loves exploring smartphones, tablets, and wearables. He began his journey with a Nokia Lumia and later dived deep into Android and iPhone. He's been writing about tech since 2018, with bylines at Pocketnow, Android Police, Pocket-Lint, and MakeUseOf. When he's not testing gadgets, he's either sipping chai, watching football, or playing cricket.

Motorola has officially detailed its upcoming Android 17 software update, which introduces new customization tools, AI-powered notification management, and enhanced display features for over 50 compatible smartphone models.

### Key Points
- Android 17 introduces stackable home screen widgets, themed icons, and the ability to hide labels within the Quick Settings menu.
- New notification features include Live Updates for real-time data and AI-driven summaries that condense long message threads into single sentences.
- Machine learning will automatically bundle low-priority alerts into a dedicated silent folder to reduce user distraction.
- Updated display settings allow users to manually adjust or disable Enhanced HDR brightness for photos and videos.
- New sharing tools, Tap to Share and Quick Drop, facilitate faster file transfers between devices.
- The update is confirmed for more than 50 Motorola devices, including recent models from the Razr and Edge product lines.

### Why it Matters
This update significantly improves the user experience by streamlining notification clutter and offering deeper customization options for the home screen. By integrating these features across a wide range of devices, Motorola ensures that a large portion of its user base benefits from modern performance and security enhancements.

articles.title: Talk Python to Me: #560: Building a Research OS: From Django to 30,000 Samples
articles.author: Michael Kennedy
articles.content:
Building a Research OS: From Django to 30,000 Samples
Guest Introduction and Background
Dr Shaun Chuah (Cher Shiong Chuah) is a gastroenterologist and clinical researcher at the University of Glasgow, where he is a Clinical Senior Research Fellow in the School of Infection and Immunity and an Honorary Consultant Gastroenterologist. His clinical practice centers on inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), the family of conditions that includes ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, and his research with the Gut Translational Research Group looks for the causes of those conditions and new treatments for the patients he sees in clinic. He also has a strong personal interest in machine learning and agentic AI, and he has been a Talk Python listener for about five years.
Shaun is not a classically trained programmer. His coding background before 2020 amounted to hand-writing HTML in Notepad in high school and a few R and Python scripts to produce graphs for statistics. When the MUSIC study he signed up for needed a way to track roughly 30,000 biological samples across multiple hospitals, he taught himself Django from the official tutorial, books, YouTube, and podcasts, and built the app himself. Six years on, that project has grown into Foundry120, a research operating system for translational science teams, complete with cloud storage, burst compute on Azure, and an agentic AI assistant named Helix.
What to Know If You're New to Python
This episode is less about Python syntax and more about what happens when you use Python to build something real that other people depend on. A little familiarity with web frameworks, cloud storage, and how modern AI agents actually work will help you follow the architecture Shaun describes.
- Django and "batteries included": Django is a mature Python web framework that ships with authentication, database migrations, and an admin interface out of the box. Shaun chose it specifically because a non-programmer could lean on those battle-tested pieces instead of building them, and it is still the backbone of Foundry120 today.
- Localhost versus production: Getting an app running on your own laptop is one thing; keeping it running securely, with backups and access controls, on a server other people rely on is a different skill. A big part of Shaun's learning curve was that jump, including learning the Linux terminal and setting up continuous deployment with GitHub Actions.
- Object storage and "everything is a file": Cloud blob storage such as Azure Blob Storage lets you store an effectively unlimited number of files and pay for what you use. Foundry120 treats every dataset, from CSV files to endoscopy videos to genomics sequencing output, as a file in blob storage with a metadata layer on top.
- Agentic AI versus chatbots: A chatbot answers a question from its training. An agentic AI system is given a task and a set of tools, then loops: it calls tools, writes and runs code, reads the results, recovers from errors, and keeps going until it has an answer. Helix, the AI inside Foundry120, works this way, much like Claude Code or Codex do for programmers.
- Role-based access control (RBAC): In clinical research, who can see which data is tightly governed. Foundry120 enforces permissions in Django so that the AI can only see exactly the files the human asking the question is allowed to see.
Key Points and Takeaways
Foundry120 is a research operating system built on three ideas: organize, centralize, and let AI operate on it
Shaun describes Foundry120 as a research operating system for translational science teams, meaning groups that recruit patients, collect samples, run experiments on them, and try to find mechanisms that could lead to new treatments. The platform rests on three ideas. First, organize your samples, studies, and participants into a single database so nothing gets lost. Second, centralize every data output in one place, whether that is clinical data like radiology images and endoscopy videos or scientific output like genomics, microbiome, and spatial transcriptomics. Third, once all that context lives in one governed platform, connect an AI to it so researchers can ask questions directly. The concrete example Shaun gives is a colleague asking whether the team has samples from any participant treated with a particular drug. Historically that meant joining a clinical dataset with the sample database by hand, a couple of days of work; with the platform, the agent can pull the data into a sandbox, write the join, and return the answer.
It all started with 30,000 samples, a spreadsheet, and the Django tutorial
In 2020, while still training as a registrar, Shaun joined a study that would recruit about 200 people across three cities and multiple hospitals, following each of them every three months and collecting blood, stool, and saliva samples at every visit. A back-of-the-envelope calculation came to roughly 30,000 samples over a couple of years. When he asked how researchers normally track that volume, the answer was Microsoft Excel. Enterprise lab systems were expensive, took months to set up, and were designed for hospital operations handling millions of samples rather than a one-off study. After surveying the off-the-shelf options, he decided the right move was to write a web app himself in Django, starting from the official tutorial. The first version was a sample-tracking system: print a QR code, stick it on a sample, scan it to register it in the database, and scan it again as it moved between sites.
Why Django: batteries included for someone who could not afford to get authentication or migrations wrong
Shaun's reasoning for choosing Django in 2020 is a good template for anyone picking a framework for a serious project without a big team. Django was mature and had been around a long time. Its authentication framework was battle tested, which matters when you are a non-programmer handling sensitive data. Its built-in database migrations meant he could evolve the schema without losing data, and in clinical research you cannot lose data. He notes that those two features alone were enough to persuade him before even counting the admin dashboard. The framework's own tagline, "the web framework for perfectionists with deadlines," matched his situation exactly: about two years to deliver a study and no time to spend forever on infrastructure. Michael also flagged fresh Django news for listeners: Django is moving to an annual release cycle with calendar-based version numbers, with every release getting long-term-support-level care, which should make the versioning simpler for newcomers to decipher.
- djangoproject.com
- djangoproject.com/weblog/2026/aug/10/annual-release-cycle
- github.com/django/deps/blob/main/accepted/0020-annual-release-cycle.rst
Books, YouTube, and the community filled the gaps for a self-taught developer
Shaun credits the Django documentation, YouTube tutorials, this podcast, and a stack of books for getting him from zero to a production app. He specifically mentions Two Scoops of Django, Obey the Testing Goat for test-driven development, Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann, and Ralph Kimball's The Data Warehouse Toolkit for dimensional modeling once the project matured into a data problem. His point about textbooks is that they give you a holistic, fundamentals-first view so you do not have gaps in what you are building, and that topics like TDD tend to live in books rather than on YouTube because they are not flashy. Michael shared that his own path was similar, coming from math into scientific research software, and that self-taught developers often have blind spots around data integrity and things like foreign key relationships. Both agreed that being aware of what you do not know, and closing those gaps deliberately, is what makes an app reliable enough for others to depend on.
- obeythetestinggoat.com
- dataintensive.net
- kimballgroup.com/data-warehouse-business-intelligence-resources/books/data-warehouse-dw-toolkit
- docs.djangoproject.com
The steepest learning curve was going from localhost to production
Running the app on a laptop was the easy part. Production meant reliable, secure, accessible infrastructure with backups, and it meant learning to operate a Linux server from a terminal when Shaun's instinct was to ask "where is the UI?" The practice that made it manageable was continuous integration and continuous deployment through GitHub Actions, so fixes could reach production in minutes rather than by hand. Michael made the case that CI/CD is at least as valuable for beginners as for big teams: if all you have to do is push to GitHub and the new version is live, a huge amount of intimidating complexity disappears. Shaun added that every time he teaches a new team member the terminal, he is reminded what a big jump the command line is for most of the population, and Michael noted that phones being most people's primary computer only widens that gap.
Ten terabytes and counting: the real problem became the data, not the samples
Tracking samples was the operational problem, but every sample then enters an experimental pipeline and produces data, and every data type looks different. Stool samples become microbiome data; blood samples become genomics data. For Shaun's own cell-free DNA sequencing work, each participant's file was 5 to 10 gigabytes of gzipped FASTQ data headed into a bioinformatics pipeline. The group currently holds about 10 terabytes, with much of the 30,000-sample backlog still unprocessed because some pipelines take a person 12 hours to handle a couple of samples. Before the platform, data was scattered across laptops, shared drives, and one-off Excel files per experiment, which Shaun calls one of the big problems in biomedical research today. Looking ahead, some newer instruments produce a terabyte of data for a single sample, grants typically cost storage for ten years, and nobody wants to rerun a 100-terabyte pipeline, so deciding which processed outputs to keep is an open question with no easy answers.
Everything is a file: blob storage plus a metadata layer as the universal data model
After years of wrestling with how to aggregate wildly different datasets into a common model, Shaun's team landed on something simple: all data exists as files in Azure Blob Storage, even tabular data, which they keep as CSV. They tried loading tables into the database in the past, but files are the universal denominator across endoscopy videos, MRI images, digital pathology slides, and sequencing output. What makes the files useful is the layer of metadata and relationship data the platform keeps on top of them. Michael pointed out that tools like DuckDB and Parquet already let you treat files like databases, and asked about embedded databases like SQLite; Shaun said they use Parquet, finds SQLite an interesting idea, but keeps CSV because his end users live in Excel and CSV. The payoff of the file model is that an AI agent can run across all of the files and pull out what it needs. Moving to blob storage also replaced the old university quota, where you emailed IT to raise a terabyte cap, with a monthly bill.
Helix is an agentic AI, not a chatbot, and that distinction is the whole point
Michael opened the AI discussion by noting that "AI" means two or three different things and people talk past each other, comparing a chatbot getting a math problem wrong with a tool-using system that writes Python to answer its questions. Helix is firmly in the second category. Shaun's description of the paradigm: you give the AI a task, it looks at its tool set and what you are trying to do, and it goes away and works until it has an answer. He estimates 95 percent of people's AI experience is closer to a Google search, so there is a huge gap in understanding how powerful agentic systems can be, and Helix is one of the first demonstrations of applying that approach in science. In the one-minute screencast on the Foundry120 site, Helix answers "what plasma samples do we have for the MUSIC study, broken down by disease group" by joining the clinical data frame with the sample database, then plots CRP against cell-free DNA by writing matplotlib code, hitting an error, reading the tool output, and correcting itself. Helix does not use a fine-tuned or retrained model; the team swaps in newer base models as they come out, because fine-tuning is expensive, needs training data that is hard to make, and does not generalize.
Django as the security guard between the AI and the data
The most distinctive architectural idea in the episode is where the permissions live. When Helix wants to process a file, the request goes through Django first: Django screens the staged code and data, spins up a VM, transfers the file from blob storage into that sandbox, runs the AI's analysis code there, and stores the output back in blob storage. The AI never calls directly into the files or the compute environment. Because the tools run on the back end, the same role-based access controls that apply to a human apply to the agent, so when a team member queries Helix, it can only see files that person could already open. Michael underlined why this matters with a story about Claude quoting his GitHub issues and offering to check something on his production server, having discovered an authenticated GitHub CLI and SSH access on its own. These agents are not malicious, but they will use any path they can find to get a better answer, so the guardrails have to be enforced outside the model.
Heavy compute stays in the cloud: 350 CPUs on Azure and embarrassingly parallel biology
Michael asked whether Pyodide or JupyterLite could push some computation into the browser to save server costs. Shaun explained why that does not fit: files are gigabytes in size and genomics pipelines are CPU and RAM hungry. Foundry120 has access to about 350 CPUs on Azure, and when a user asks Helix for a heavy transcriptomics analysis, Django orchestrates a compute job that spins up as many CPUs as needed, runs for anywhere from half an hour to a couple of hours, and returns the result later. Many biological problems are naturally parallel: with 200 participants at 5 gigabytes each, you might as well spin up 200 machines, process everything at once, and tear it all down, which he sums up as minimal cost for maximum impact. There is a second reason to keep compute server-side: the platform runs sample collection in hospitals across Scotland, where front-line IT is not always the best and some machines date to 2010 on decade-old chips, so a server-rendered app guarantees a fast experience regardless of the client.
Django REST Framework on the back end, TypeScript and React on the front end
The original app was pure Django with Django templates handling registration and CRUD workflows. As the platform moved into AI, Shaun rebuilt the front end in TypeScript and React talking to a Django REST Framework back end. His reasoning is that AI is inherently asynchronous: every model call can take what feels like forever, and running an agent loop involves many such calls, which JavaScript and TypeScript are well suited to handle interactively. He calls the combination a great setup because it gives the team the entire Python data science ecosystem on the back end and the full TypeScript and JavaScript ecosystem for the interactive, async-heavy front end that AI applications need.
Governance decides everything: where inference runs, why there is no MCP server, and why you cannot just sign up
Foundry120 runs on the University of Glasgow's Azure tenancy, with most workloads in the UK South data center and EU-compliant work in Sweden. All inference happens inside Azure under GDPR-compliant controls, which is why, when Michael asked about adding an MCP server so people could query Foundry from their own AI tools, Shaun said the limiting factor is governance: they are not allowed to put patient data into Claude Code and send it to Anthropic. The same constraints shape who can use the platform. Over the last six to twelve months the foundation has been made generalizable beyond Shaun's group and beyond IBD, with team management and permission assignment built in, but onboarding is a hands-on process that depends on data types, volumes, modalities, and each study's research ethics approval. That is why the site offers a platform walkthrough rather than a self-serve monthly subscription. Michael noted that GDPR applies to US companies with European customers as well, and that this same territory covers IRB approvals and HIPAA in the States.
Cloud versus the basement cluster: the economics of research computing and AI
Michael reflected on how universities have gone from a Cray or Silicon Graphics machine in a basement to renting effectively unlimited cloud capacity. Shaun argued the cloud is far more cost-efficient for universities because most analyses are one-off bursts: you might process a huge dataset once every year or two, which is a poor fit for owning hardware that sits idle in between. He is even more definitive about AI, where a single NVIDIA rack costs a couple of million dollars and needs a power plant to plug into; he cannot see any university building its own AI data center, so cloud adoption is inevitable unless specific governance requirements force otherwise, and even then a shared local provider makes more sense than each university going alone. The two also speculated about the future: Michael suggested that if frontier subscriptions became dramatically more expensive, a ten-thousand-dollar local workstation would suddenly look like a bargain, and imagined an orchestration layer routing to small domain-specialist models. Shaun agreed small models are getting more capable and not every workload needs a frontier model.
The job changes from writing the analysis to verifying it
Historically, every new team member had to sit down with Shaun and learn enough Python or R to get a graph out of an Excel file. Now they can hand that to Helix and let it write the code, and their job becomes checking that the result is correct. Shaun is candid that the reliability threshold has not been crossed: even the best models like Opus and Fable still make mistakes, so understanding what you are trying to do matters more today than it did five years ago, because you have to know enough to supervise the AI. He tells his scientific colleagues that answers must pass the smell test and land in the expected magnitude range, and that disposable work can be delegated more freely while critical workflows need every step verified. Michael's counterpoint is that humans are not 100 percent reliable either, and people expect perfection from AI because software has always been deterministic. He pointed to the recent tension around AI pre-screening of Linux kernel patches as an example of that expectation clashing with a tool that is often as good as the people doing the job. Shaun's framing: an AI is like a colleague who writes code faster and better than most people, but the human still supplies the strategic view and the direction.
Most of the world has never touched a coding agent, and closing that gap is the real work
Shaun's read on the next few years is optimistic but grounded. Agentic AI has a genuine role in shortening bottlenecks in drug discovery and will transform how science and clinical work are done, but the real world will take a while to catch up to today's capabilities. Most Talk Python listeners have used a coding agent; almost everybody else in the population has not. Scientists he demos Helix to are often seeing an agentic system for the first time, and their reaction is that work which used to take months or a long email chain now takes minutes. His closing call to action is generous: the team does not yet know whether Foundry120 generalizes beyond their group or stays hyper-personal software, so he has shared the principles widely and encourages other institutions to take the ideas and build their own, while inviting anyone interested in a partnership to reach out through the website.
Interesting Quotes and Stories
"When I first visited the Django website, it said the web framework for perfectionists with deadlines. And I think that described exactly the situation I was in." -- Shaun Chuah
"I wasn't very good of a programmer. What I did was basically write some websites in high school. And back in those days, we used to use Notepad. We used to open the brackets of HTML manually by hand." -- Shaun Chuah
"A simple back of the envelope calculation came to about 30,000 samples that we were going to generate over a couple of years. When I first saw that challenge, I started asking everybody around me, how are we going to keep track of all that? The common way that researchers track the samples is to use Microsoft Excel." -- Shaun Chuah
"You have a bill instead of a limit." -- Michael Kennedy, on moving from university storage quotas to Azure Blob Storage
"Some of the newer technologies are generating like a terabyte of data for a single sample." -- Shaun Chuah
"Who wants to run another 100 terabyte pipeline anyway?" -- Shaun Chuah, on deciding which processed outputs to keep
"We've actually put a Django in as a security guard between your AI and the raw data and the compute environments that we run." -- Shaun Chuah
"These AIs are sneaky. They will find a way to access the files." -- Michael Kennedy

"So the work changes. Instead of you as a researcher writing the analysis code, you get the AI to do the analysis for you. And then what you have to do is verify that it is correct." -- Shaun Chuah
"Having an AI by your side is like having a colleague on your team. Except this colleague can write code tremendously faster and much better than most people." -- Shaun Chuah
"Because it's a computer, people expect it to be perfect. Software is typically deterministic. So if it works once, it's always going to work. And AI isn't like that. But people also aren't like that." -- Michael Kennedy

"Please feel free to just take the idea and run with it." -- Shaun Chuah
The Silicon Graphics machine that ran out of bytes. Michael told a story from his university days in a math research lab, where the whole department shared a Silicon Graphics mainframe with no disk quotas. A grad student debugging their code added logging, accidentally created an infinite loop, and left it running overnight. By morning the machine would not respond, and it took a day or two to figure out why: the log had filled the hard drive to the very last byte, and the operating system needed a few temp files to function. Shaun's takeaway, delivered with a laugh, was that those limits have a reason to exist.
Claude finds the GitHub CLI. While working with Claude on his code, Michael was surprised when it referenced two GitHub issues he had never given it access to. It had noticed the GitHub CLI was installed and already authenticated because Michael had logged in at some point, so it simply used that. Later it offered to check something on his production server, having worked out from the code that it could SSH in. His point was that these tools are not malicious, they are just trying to give you a better answer, but "we fixed the problem by resetting the database" is a real risk if the guardrails are not enforced outside the model.
Key Definitions and Terms
- Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD): A group of chronic conditions, principally ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, in which the immune system reacts to the environment and the inflammation never switches off. Shaun describes it as rare but growing in both developed and developing countries.
- Translational science: Research that recruits people with a condition, collects samples, runs lab experiments to understand the biology of disease, and looks for mechanisms that could be targeted for new treatments. Foundry120 is built for teams doing this kind of work.
- MUSIC study: The multi-site IBD biomarker study at the University of Glasgow's Gut Translational Research Group that Foundry120 grew out of. Its projected 30,000 samples were the original reason Shaun learned Django.
- Helix: The agentic AI assistant inside Foundry120. It uses tools to query samples and clinical data, writes and runs analysis code in a sandbox, and recovers from its own errors.
- Agentic AI: An AI system that is given a task and a set of tools, then works autonomously through a loop of tool calls, code execution, and self-correction until it produces an answer. Contrasted in the episode with chatbots, which are closer to a search engine.
- Role-based access control (RBAC): A permissions model where what a user can see and do is determined by their role. Foundry120 enforces RBAC in Django, and the AI inherits exactly the permissions of the person asking.
- Sandbox: An isolated compute environment, in Foundry120's case a VM spun up on demand, where AI-generated code runs against a copy of the data so the agent never touches the raw storage or production systems directly.
- Azure Blob Storage: Microsoft's cloud object storage service. Foundry120 keeps every data file there, replacing scattered laptops, shared drives, and university storage quotas with pay-as-you-go storage.
- Microsoft Foundry: Microsoft's platform for building and governing AI apps and agents on Azure. Michael references it alongside Azure as part of the stack Foundry120 has integrated with.
- CI/CD (continuous integration and continuous deployment): The practice of automatically testing and deploying code on every push. Shaun uses GitHub Actions so fixes reach production in minutes.
- Django REST Framework: A toolkit for building web APIs on top of Django. Foundry120's TypeScript and React front end talks to Django through it.
- Calendar versioning (CalVer): A version numbering scheme based on the release date. Django is adopting it as part of its move to annual releases, so future versions will be named for their year rather than incrementing 5.2, 6.0, and so on.
- FASTQ: A text-based file format for DNA sequencing reads and their quality scores, usually gzipped. Shaun's cell-free DNA files arrive this way at 5 to 10 gigabytes per participant.
- Cell-free DNA: DNA fragments circulating freely in the blood. Sequencing it was the focus of Shaun's personal research project within the MUSIC study.
- CRP (C-reactive protein): A common blood test marker of inflammation. In the Helix demo, it is plotted against cell-free DNA levels.
- Parquet: A columnar file format widely used in data engineering that tools like DuckDB can query directly. Shaun's team uses it alongside CSV.
- Pyodide and JupyterLite: Pyodide is a port of CPython to WebAssembly that runs Python in the browser; JupyterLite is a JupyterLab distribution built on it that needs no server. Michael raised them as a way to offload compute to the client, which does not fit Foundry120's gigabyte-scale workloads.
- Model Context Protocol (MCP): An open standard for connecting AI assistants to external tools and data sources. Michael suggested a Foundry MCP server, which governance rules currently rule out.
- GDPR: The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation. It is the reason all Foundry120 inference stays inside Azure data centers in the UK and Sweden.
- Dimensional modeling: The data warehouse design approach from Ralph Kimball's The Data Warehouse Toolkit, which Shaun read as the project shifted from sample tracking to data management.
Learning Resources
If this episode has you thinking about building a Django app for your own research group, wiring an agent up to real data, or simply understanding how tool-using AI works under the hood, here are some places to go deeper.
- Django: Getting Started: Build a real Django app from the ground up, covering the models, migrations, authentication, and admin features that convinced Shaun Django was the right choice for a non-programmer with a deadline.
- Agentic AI Programming for Python: Learn to work effectively with coding agents like Claude Code and Codex, the same style of tool-using AI that Helix brings to scientific research.
- LLM Building Blocks for Python: A practical introduction to programming against LLMs from Python, including tool use and structured outputs, the foundations of building an agent like Helix on your own data.
- docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/intro/tutorial01: The official Django tutorial, which is exactly where Shaun started in 2020.
- obeythetestinggoat.com: Harry Percival's Test-Driven Development with Python, free to read online, and one of the books Shaun credits for closing his testing gaps.
- dataintensive.net: Martin Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications, recommended by Shaun for understanding the fundamentals of data systems.
- djangoproject.com/weblog/2026/aug/10/annual-release-cycle: The Django announcement Michael mentioned, explaining the move to annual, calendar-versioned releases.
- foundry120.com: The Foundry120 site, including the one-minute Helix screencast narrated in the episode and the platform walkthrough request.
Overall Takeaway
Shaun Chuah's story is a reminder that the most consequential software is often built by the person closest to the problem, not the person with the most credentials in programming. A doctor who had last written HTML by hand in Notepad looked at 30,000 samples and a spreadsheet, opened the Django tutorial, and kept going. Six years later that decision has become a governed research platform holding 10 terabytes of clinical and genomics data, orchestrating hundreds of CPUs on Azure, and giving scientists an AI colleague that answers in minutes what used to take days of manual joins.
The technical lessons are just as portable as the personal ones. Pick boring, battle-tested foundations when the stakes are high. Treat every dataset as a file with metadata on top so that both humans and agents can reason over it. Keep permissions and guardrails in your own code, in Shaun's case Django standing between the AI and the data, rather than trusting the model to stay in its lane. And when you hand analysis to an agent, understand that your job has not disappeared; it has shifted to supervision and verification. As Shaun puts it, most of the world has never touched a coding agent yet. If you are a Python developer who has, you are unusually well placed to close that gap for the scientists, clinicians, and researchers around you, and to take these ideas and run with them.

articles.summary:
Gastroenterologist Dr. Shaun Chuah developed Foundry120, a research operating system built with Django that leverages agentic AI to manage 30,000 biological samples and 10 terabytes of clinical research data.

### Key Points
- Foundry120 uses Django for secure, role-based access control and Azure Blob Storage to centralize diverse datasets like genomics and endoscopy videos.
- The platform integrates Helix, an agentic AI assistant that autonomously writes and executes Python code to analyze data within isolated, secure virtual machine sandboxes.
- Dr. Chuah built the system to replace manual, error-prone tracking in Microsoft Excel, enabling researchers to perform complex data joins and analysis in minutes.
- The architecture prioritizes data governance and security by keeping all inference and compute within the University of Glasgow’s compliant Azure cloud environment.
- The platform supports high-performance, parallelized bioinformatics pipelines, utilizing hundreds of Azure CPUs to process large-scale datasets on demand.

### Why it Matters
- This project demonstrates how domain experts can build sophisticated, production-grade research infrastructure by leveraging battle-tested frameworks and cloud-native tools. It highlights a shift in scientific workflows where the researcher's role evolves from manual data processing to supervising and verifying AI-driven analysis.

articles.title: The Features That Make a Cryptocurrency Android App Worth Using
articles.author: AndroidGuys
articles.content:
Most people don’t think about how much they rely on apps until something stops working. Banking, shopping, travel and entertainment are all handled from a phone now, often with just a few taps.
Cryptocurrency has moved in the same direction. Instead of sitting at a desktop computer to check digital assets or review account activity, people can manage many parts of their cryptocurrency experience through Android apps.
Someone checking the Bitcoin price, for example, may only want a quick update while they’re out and about. Platforms such as Binance have helped make this type of access easier by bringing cryptocurrency tools directly to mobile devices. But downloading an app is only the beginning. With so many cryptocurrency platforms available, the way an app feels to use can be just as important as the features it offers.
Making cryptocurrency easier to follow
Cryptocurrency can feel complicated when someone is first getting started. There are new terms to learn, different types of assets to understand and plenty of information available at the same time.
A mobile app can make that first experience feel less overwhelming. Checking a balance, reviewing transactions or looking at market changes should feel straightforward rather than like a search through endless menus.
The layout of an app matters more than people often realise. A confusing design can turn a simple task into a frustrating one, while a well-organised interface lets people move around naturally.
But a simple design doesn’t mean an app should feel limited. Someone new to cryptocurrency may want a clear overview, while someone with more experience may be looking for charts, portfolio tracking or more detailed market information.
The difficult part is bringing those different needs together. Advanced tools have their place, but they shouldn’t make everyday actions harder.
Keeping information clear and up to date
One of the main reasons people use cryptocurrency apps is convenience. Markets move throughout the day, and having information available on a phone means users don’t need to search through different websites every time they want an update.
Someone following daily price changes may want a quick overview before checking back later. Another person may only open an app when they want to review their portfolio or check recent activity.
Having access to more information sounds useful, but it can also create problems. A busy screen full of charts, numbers and updates may leave someone unsure about what they should actually be looking at.
The way information is arranged can change how useful it feels. A simple overview may tell someone more than a page filled with figures they don’t immediately understand.
Notifications can be helpful, although they’re easy to overdo. A useful alert can remind someone about an update they care about, but too many messages can make people switch them off completely.
Apps also need ongoing updates. Developers need to fix issues and improve performance. This is to make sure the app continues working properly as Android devices and software change.
That is particularly important for Android users because there is such a wide range of devices available. A cryptocurrency app may be used on a high-end smartphone one day and a more affordable model the next.
What makes a cryptocurrency app feel reliable
Security is one of the first things people think about when using any financial app. Cryptocurrency is no different. Giving an app access to digital assets is a big step. So security features are usually one of the first things people look for.
Options like two-factor authentication, biometric login and account alerts allow users to choose how they can protect their accounts. But these features only really work when people know where to find them. If security settings feel hidden or complicated, they may not be used regularly.
Speed and reliability is also important. A platform might include useful tools, but slow loading times, delayed updates or failed actions can quickly become frustrating.
This is especially important for financial apps. People expect information to load correctly and everyday actions to work without delays. Performance is also important for Android users. Unlike some other mobile systems, Android runs across many different devices with different hardware, screen sizes and software versions.
Why mobile has become central to cryptocurrency
The way people use online services has changed significantly. Banking, shopping, entertainment and communication have all moved heavily towards mobile apps.
As of 2026, 88% of all mobile internet time is spent inside applications rather than mobile web browsers. Apps have become the main way many people interact with digital services.
Cryptocurrency has followed the same path. For many people, an Android app is now the easiest way to stay connected to their digital assets. Extra features can be useful too. Educational resources, portfolio tools and price alerts may appeal to different types of users depending on what they want from the app.
But having more options doesn’t automatically create a better experience. An app can offer dozens of tools and still feel difficult if the basics aren’t easy to use.
The features people return to are usually the ones that save time. Quick access to information, reliable performance and a layout that makes sense are what turn an app from something people download into something they regularly use.
A cryptocurrency Android app doesn’t need to make every task complicated. The most useful experiences are often the ones that make managing digital assets feel simple.

articles.title: Meta's historic $18 billion settlement may mean little for the plight of teens
articles.author: Amanda Hoover
articles.content:
On Wednesday, Meta reached an agreement with attorneys general across states, Washington, DC, and US territories that had brought claims the design of the company's apps had harmed children. The company will pay up to $18 billion in penalties and alter its apps to potentially limit the amount of time teens spend on them daily.
The settlement is historic: It's the highest ever paid to states by a Big Tech company, and it could have massive implications for how other social media companies design their platforms for both kids and adult users.
What we don't yet know is whether the specific changes Meta has agreed to implement will alleviate what brought on the lawsuit in the first place: the problems teens face when they log on to social media.
The company will install interruptions to infinite scroll, impose two-hour daily time limits for using its apps, and silence notifications overnight and during the school day. Meta has also agreed to limit the use of beauty filters and hide the tallying of likes on posts by default, while strengthening age verification tools and parental controls. The agreement also allows teens to choose a non-algorithmic feed, harkening back to the early days of social media, and turn off autoplay, meaning they would have to tap or swipe to see specific content.
Meta lost two lawsuits this year regarding safety on its platforms. Now, the company has taken a more proactive stance in revamping their products, says Stavros Gadinis, a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law. "Their strategy is developing," he says, because they may believe that by embracing these changes, "they're going to convince consumers that their product is credible."
The settlement aims for an issue that lawmakers and parents have sounded alarms on, but it could miss the mark. Giant social media companies get blamed for the state of the modern world, but mere usage is not the root cause of issues teens face. Because social media is a highly visible target, it's drawn ire. People think: "These are the bad guys, we gotta go after them," says Ari Lightman, a professor at Carnegie Mellon University's Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy. "The bad guys are unfortunately everywhere."
Approaches that track and limit kids' time on the internet don't address the deeper issues that draw them online and lead them to have a negative experience. Those fixes may cost more than the whopping $18 billion. "We don't provide really good programs associated with digital citizenship, with cyber hygiene," as an essential part of the K-12 school system, Lightman says.
Cody Venzke, senior staff attorney at the ACLU, has concerns about the settlement's practical implications. He sees it as a way to "sidestep the First Amendment by implementing these requirements through a settlement agreement as opposed to the legislative process." Venzke argues that an age verification mandate for certain content will lead Meta to verify the ages of all its users. These measures can erode privacy online.
The ACLU has opposed laws that could lead to age verification, arguing that blocking teens from accessing social media violates free speech protections. The settlement can lead Meta to block access to content for both teens and those who don't comply with age verification on its platforms, while also collecting more data on all of its users in a way that has "enshrined that surveillance as a measure to protect kids."
Meta said in its statement today that it wants "to get this right for parents and teens, and that's why we partnered with state attorneys general to set a new industry standard," and that the agreement builds "on our longstanding efforts to empower parents and support teens." The company's stock rose by about 1% following news of the settlement.
People think: "These are the bad guys, we gotta go after them. The bad guys are unfortunately everywhere," says Ari Lightman.
The dominant refrain in recent years has been that screens and social media have ruined childhood, addicting kids and harming their mental health. But a report from the US Surgeon General's Office in 2023 noted that there are also benefits — such helping teens find community and express their creativity — and "we do not yet have enough evidence to determine if social media is sufficiently safe for children and adolescents."
More recent research has pushed back on the destruction of childhood narrative. The University of Manchester tracked 25,000 kids' social media and gaming habits over a three-year period, and found "no evidence" that more frequent social media use or gaming activity led to an increase in anxiety and depression over the next year. Another from the University of Toronto found that LGBTQ teens can benefit from social media for emotional support, education, and research. A study published last year in Scientific Reports found that people often overestimate their "addiction" to social media, which is more often habitual than comparable to an addiction to a substance like nicotine. "Continued overuse of this terminology risks stigmatizing healthy usage, wasting public health resources, and contributing to moral panic around social media use," the researchers wrote.
In its blogpost announcing the settlement, Meta called on its competitors, like YouTube and TikTok, to follow its lead: "While this is an important step, the fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day. All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place, because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another." The agreement says that Meta will pay more money if TikTok and YouTube also agree to similar restrictions for teens, and also pay $5 billion each.
Meta knows it needs eyes. Corralling its competitors to also kick teens off their apps after an hour a day would level the playing field in a competitive attention economy, and broaden the civil liberties concerns that Venzke raised across larger swaths of the web.
Wednesday's settlement continues a trend this year of Meta facing some accountability for its platform design, a consequence that tech companies previously skirted. We've all been living in the great social media experiment for the past two decades, during which Meta has always survived and taken on new forms. Now, it's setting the tone for the experiment's next era.
Amanda Hoover is a senior correspondent at Business Insider covering the tech industry. She writes about the biggest tech companies and trends.
Business Insider's Discourse stories provide perspectives on the day's most pressing issues, informed by analysis, reporting, and expertise.
articles.summary:
Meta has reached a historic $18 billion settlement with US states to resolve claims that its app designs harm children by implementing new teen safety and usage restrictions.

### Key Points
- Meta will introduce two-hour daily time limits, overnight notification silences, and interruptions to infinite scrolling for teen users.
- The company agreed to hide like counts by default, limit beauty filters, and provide options for non-algorithmic content feeds.
- This settlement represents the largest payout by a Big Tech company to state attorneys general regarding platform safety concerns.
- Meta is calling on competitors like TikTok and YouTube to adopt similar safety standards to ensure consistent protections across the industry.
- Privacy advocates, including the ACLU, warn that mandatory age verification requirements could lead to increased data collection and potential First Amendment violations.

### Why it Matters
This settlement sets a significant legal precedent that could force other social media platforms to overhaul their design features to prioritize teen mental health. While the agreement aims to curb digital addiction, it also raises complex questions about the balance between protecting minors and maintaining user privacy across the internet.

articles.title: Apple Maps Has Ads Now. They Might Not Be Terrible, but You Can’t Turn Them Off
articles.author: Omar Gallaga
articles.content:
Apple, as expected, has introduced advertisements into its Maps navigation app, though you might not notice them at first.
The company confirmed in March it would bring ads to Maps and other services, including Mail, Wallet and Siri, as part of an Apple Business platform it launched in April. The ads are expected to roll out for Maps in the US and Canada before appearing in other regions.
The only way to tell that you’re seeing a paid advertisement in Maps, at least for now, is a very small “ad” marker. Suggested locations appear alongside ones that aren’t marked as ads.
In CNET’s testing, ads in Maps only appeared next to some search results, and unlike what you’d see in Google Maps, there are so far no sponsored pins. Not every search result showed ads, even in highly populated areas like New York City and San Francisco. So at least on the initial rollout, users might not notice a major design change.
But many say this isn’t a good look for the tech giant. One headline on the popular site 9to5 Mac called the Maps ads “as bad as expected.” The other concern? Apple hasn’t introduced an opt-out toggle for ads, so you can’t even turn them off.
Apple customers on a subreddit devoted to the company were not happy about the ad rollout, with some arguing that paid iCloud account holders should not have to see ads. Others complained about advertising being introduced into the App Store, News and other applications. “This ad overload on everything is getting unbearable,” wrote MarkE2020.
Digital Noise on X predicted that this isn’t the end of Apple’s advertising push. “Music is next,” they wrote.
Apple ads and privacy
As part of the ad rollout, Apple posted about how it’s handling privacy: “Our advertising platform is designed to protect users’ information and give them control over how we use it for advertising.”
The post states that Apple Ads doesn’t buy or share personal information with other companies, doesn’t track users across apps and websites owned by other companies, and doesn’t serve ads to users registered as under 13 years old. Apple Pay transactions, Health app data and Home app data aren’t used to deliver ads.
A representative for Apple pointed CNET to its post about Maps ad privacy, but didn’t comment on whether information from other apps might be used or if it uses anonymized or aggregated user data for its ad business.
In a bid for transparency, Apple says that clicking the “ad” icon shows the information used to serve the ad.
Google vs. Apple navigation tools
At the time of its announcement, there was speculation about how closely Apple’s ad approach would resemble what is seen in Google Maps. Tim Berney, founder and CEO of Oklahoma City-based VI Marketing and Branding, told CNET that Apple is playing a different game and its Maps ads wouldn’t be identical to Google, which seems to be the case.
“Apple will likely take a more subtle, integrated approach,” Berney said. “Where Google Maps or Waze can feel more ad-driven, Apple will make it feel like a recommendation within the experience,” he said.
Some commentators online have speculated whether advertising in Apple Maps is purely a revenue play. But because the move is positioned as part of Apple’s small-business toolset, Berney said ads could be a way for Apple to lure business owners into its own ecosystem of apps and device management platforms. And that would, not coincidentally, put it in direct competition with Google.
articles.summary:
Apple has officially introduced subtle, marked advertisements into its Maps navigation application, beginning with a rollout across the United States and Canada for business-related search results.

### Key Points
- Apple is integrating paid advertisements into Maps search results, identified by a small "ad" label.
- The rollout currently targets the United States and Canada, with no sponsored pins appearing in initial tests.
- Apple has not provided an opt-out toggle for users to disable these advertisements within the application.
- The company maintains that its advertising platform does not track users across third-party apps or share personal data.
- Apple positions these ads as part of a broader business platform designed to support small-business discovery.

### Why it Matters
This expansion signals a strategic shift for Apple as it seeks to grow its advertising revenue while competing directly with Google’s established navigation ecosystem. By integrating these tools, Apple aims to draw more small businesses into its proprietary software and device management platforms.

articles.title: Gatik has raised $200m to put more driverless box trucks on US roads
articles.author: Cristian Dina
articles.content:
Gatik has raised $200m in a Series D round led by Qatar Investment Authority and Koch Disruptive Technologies. It is the largest financing in the autonomous trucking company’s history. Millennium Management, ARK Invest and Intact Private Capital also took part, and the round brings Gatik’s total to about $500m since it came out of stealth in 2019. The company declined to disclose its valuation.
David Welch interviewed the chief executive for Bloomberg on Tuesday. The Santa Clara company set out the round the same day in a company release.
What the company says it has already sold
Gatik puts its contracted revenue above $600m. It says it has completed 85,000 fully driverless orders at 99% on-time delivery. Chief executive and co-founder Gautam Narang told Bloomberg in January that the company had signed deals worth $600m over five years, and he said this week that the backlog has grown since. He would not say by how much, and he declined to say whether Gatik is profitable.
The niche is the middle mile
Gatik moves freight between distribution centres and stores. It does not do long-haul, robotaxis or sidewalk delivery. Kirsten Korosec set out the history at TechCrunch. The company began with fixed routes under ten miles, and now runs dynamic routes with dozens of pick-up and drop-off points covering up to 400 miles.
The box trucks come from Isuzu Motors, and Gatik supplies the driving system it calls the Gatik Driver. Narang told TechCrunch the third-generation trucks run around the clock on surface streets and motorways. They can handle light rain and snow.
Who it drives for
Walmart was the first customer, disclosed in 2019, and PepsiCo, Kroger and Tyson Foods followed. The PepsiCo agreement, signed in June, is the largest public one. Forty-one driverless box trucks move Frito-Lay products from distribution centres to stores in Dallas, Phoenix and Northwest Arkansas, and Gatik calls it its biggest commercial deployment so far.
The company also runs for Loblaw in Ontario, where a safety driver is still behind the wheel. Its trucks operate nearly around the clock, carrying ambient, refrigerated and frozen goods. Its customers are Fortune 50 retail, grocery and consumer packaged goods companies, according to the release.
The fleet numbers do not sit still
Gatik says it has dozens of driverless trucks running today and plans to expand to thousands in the years ahead. A spokesperson told Reuters the target is more than 100 by the end of 2026. Narang told Forbes in January that the fleet would go from fewer than a dozen to hundreds of box trucks by the end of this year.
The driverless routes run in the Dallas and Fort Worth region, Phoenix and Northwest Arkansas. Gatik pulled its safety drivers from commercial routes last year, which is what made those operations possible. The release describes the routes as high-frequency regional networks, time-sensitive and operationally complex.
What the money is for
Narang said the round funds more trucks, more customers and more cities. Gatik will hire engineers and operational staff on top of its 350-person workforce, and will expand both into new markets and further inside the ones it already serves.
“These are very sophisticated long-term financial investors that usually get involved when the business is proven out and the economics are proven out,” he told Bloomberg. “It’s less about building a business. It’s more about scaling the business that we have today.”
What the investors said
Cathie Wood, who runs ARK Invest, said autonomous freight is reaching an inflection point as AI and robotics converge. Abdulla Al-Kuwari, head of industrials at QIA, said the fund is backing companies shaping the future of freight infrastructure.
Byron Knight, president of Koch Disruptive Technologies, said autonomy is moving beyond a promising technology into real-world commercial operations. His colleague Celeste Dauner said the firm first backed Gatik in 2021 and has watched it build scale around a focused application. Justin Smith-Lorenzetti of Intact Private Capital said his firm has tripled its commitment with this round, and ARK’s Tasha Keeney said autonomous trucking should meaningfully lower the cost of transporting goods.
Europe is not on the map yet
Gatik operates in Texas, Arizona, Arkansas and Canada. Its site also lists California, Michigan, Nebraska, Iowa and Ontario. Narang told TechCrunch that scaling means more trucks, customers and cities, and someday operations outside North America. Reuters reported interest in driverless commercial freight surging in both North America and Europe.
No European route has been announced, and the company has not said which market would come first. Waymo said this month it is laying groundwork in Munich for late 2027, though that is passenger service rather than freight.
The European trucking comparison
Einride is the closest European name, and it took a different route. It listed on Nasdaq in June at $1.35bn, below the $5bn it had once discussed with banks. This month it agreed to buy 500 Tesla Semis, with Amazon holding a stake in the buyer.
Rivian’s spinout Also raised $150m this month, and Waymo built its own chip. Capital is moving across the whole autonomy stack rather than one part of it.
What to watch
Gatik has not published a valuation, a profit figure or a precise fleet count. Its release carries a forward-looking statements disclaimer covering the revenue targets, the customer base and the fleet plans, and notes the securities were sold in a transaction exempt from registration.
The company says it will reach thousands of trucks, while Reuters has it at more than 100 by December. Loblaw in Ontario remains the one operation still carrying a safety driver, and Gatik has not said when that changes.

articles.summary:
Autonomous trucking company Gatik has secured $200 million in Series D funding to scale its middle-mile logistics operations and expand its fleet of driverless box trucks across North America.

### Key Points
- The $200 million funding round was led by Qatar Investment Authority and Koch Disruptive Technologies, bringing Gatik’s total capital raised to approximately $500 million.
- Gatik reports over $600 million in contracted revenue and has completed 85,000 fully driverless deliveries for major clients including Walmart, PepsiCo, Kroger, and Tyson Foods.
- The company utilizes Isuzu box trucks equipped with the proprietary "Gatik Driver" system to transport goods between distribution centers and retail stores.
- Current driverless operations are concentrated in Texas, Arizona, and Arkansas, with plans to grow the fleet from dozens to over 100 trucks by the end of 2026.
- The new capital will support hiring additional engineering and operational staff while funding expansion into new geographic markets and increasing truck production.

### Why it Matters
This significant investment signals growing institutional confidence in the commercial viability of autonomous middle-mile logistics as a solution for complex, high-frequency supply chain networks. By focusing on specific regional routes rather than long-haul trucking, Gatik is positioning itself to scale rapidly within the retail and consumer goods sectors.

articles.title: Hands-On: Sonnet Echo 21 Thunderbolt 5 SuperDock – a significant speed boost [Video]
articles.author: Jeff Benjamin
articles.content:
The Sonnet Echo 21 Thunderbolt 5 SuperDock, the follow-up to the similarly named Echo 20 Thunderbolt 4 SuperDock (review), lets you add tons of I/O to your Mac via a single Thunderbolt cable, and brings several noteworthy improvements for those looking to upgrade or future-proof their Mac setups.
Perfect for both laptops like the MacBook Pro, and desktop machines like the just-announced M5 Pro Mac mini, the Echo 21 SuperDock adds a vast array of I/O to these machines. Watch our full hands-on video walkthrough for the details, and be sure to subscribe to 9to5mac on YouTube for more.
Specifications
- 1 x Thunderbolt 5 upstream port
- 2 x Thunderbolt 5 downstream ports
- 140W Power Delivery to upstream host
- 10Gb Ethernet
- Nine 10Gbps USB 3 ports
- One 15W and three 7.5W charging ports
- 24-bit/192 kHz audio with headset, stereo line out, and mic in
- SD and microSD UHS-II 4.0 slots
- M.2 SSD socket for up to 8TB of additional storage
- Supports up to three displays via HDMI, DP, or two Thunderbolt 5 ports
- Price $499, available now
Video: Sonnet Echo 21 Thunderbolt 5 SuperDock
What’s new?
How does the Echo 21 Thunderbolt 5 SuperDock compare to its direct predecessor? If you were just to take a quick glance, you’d be hard-pressed to tell the difference between the two. The design, form factor, color, and virtually everything else about these two devices look the same. But upon closer inspection, it’s clear the Thunderbolt 5 SuperDock adds a helping of new features to enhance workflows.
Thunderbolt 5 ports
The most noteworthy benefit of the Echo 21 over its predecessor is that all Thunderbolt ports have been upgraded from Thunderbolt 4 to Thunderbolt 5. This is a substantial upgrade, as Thunderbolt 5 supports double the bandwidth of Thunderbolt 4, increasing from up to 40 Gbps to up to 80 Gbps of bidirectional data. You’ll notice the difference when transferring data between both the internal and externally mounted SSDs if connected to a Thunderbolt 5 machine.
Thunderbolt 5 connectivity also supports Bandwidth Boost, which dynamically reallocates some downstream lane capacity to the upstream lane when necessary. Under certain conditions, this reallocation may peak at up to 120 Gbps on the upstream side. This dynamic bandwidth allocation enables connecting to displays with high resolutions and refresh rates that require extra throughput.
One interesting thing that eagle-eyed users will notice is that there are actually four ports listed in System Information for the dock’s Thunderbolt 5 controller. Port A is the upstream port to the host computer, and ports B and D are the downstream ports. So, where does that leave Port C? That particular port, although not tied to a physical USB-C connection, is used for the DisplayPort/HDMI output.
DisplayPort
Notably, Sonnet adds a full-size DisplayPort connection to the Thunderbolt 5 SuperDock, a feature not available on the Thunderbolt 4 version. It means the dock can now connect to a display via Thunderbolt/USB-C, HDMI, or DisplayPort. Note that you can use only HDMI or DisplayPort; it’s either/or, not both, and HDMI takes precedence when both are connected. When connecting via HDMI, connectivity tops out at 4K60, so I recommend using DisplayPort, which supports up to 4K144. If you’re looking for the most capable connectivity option, use Thunderbolt, which supports a wider range of resolutions and frame rates.
Upstream Thunderbolt port
Because Thunderbolt 5 has a minimum mandatory power delivery requirement of 140W, it can deliver full power to a power-hungry machine like the 16-inch MacBook Pro, while the Thunderbolt 4 version of the dock was limited to 100W. This change also means that the power adapter that drives the dock is now larger and rated for higher power: 20V at 12A vs 20V at 7.5A.
10Gb Ethernet
One of the main complaints I heard in response to my Echo 20 SuperDock review was about the lack of 10GbE. Sonnet has allayed these concerns with the Echo 21 SuperDock, which uses a Marvell AQC113 chipset to deliver high-performance connectivity up to 10 Gbps at relatively low power. The chipset also supports GbE, 2.5GbE, and 5GbE, which is handy when connecting to a NAS or other devices with those options.
Hi-res audio
The Echo 21 SuperDock features an upgraded hi-resolution codec that supports the audio ports, enabling lossless audio up to 24-bit/192 kHz. So if you’re the type who can discern the difference between lossless audio files, you’ll be happy with this upgrade. With that said, I currently use a Rode Rodecaster Duo as an audio interface and mixer, but if ever in a pinch, the Echo 21 lets me connect directly to my powered Yamaha HS3 monitors for full audio output.
microSD
In the past, I’ve tended to overlook microSD support, always feeling like it was a superfluous addition. But as I add more devices to my workflow that use this storage medium, like the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 and the aforementioned Rode Rodecaster Duo, I’m grateful for its inclusion. No finagling with microSD → SD Card adapters, just insert the microSD card and be done with it.
Front-facing USB-C port with 15W power output
The Echo 21 SuperDock includes a third front-facing USB-C port, bringing the total to five front-facing USB ports. But unlike the initial four USB-A and USB-C ports, this added port can charge devices up to 15W – double the speed of the other four ports on the front. This is handy for charging a smartphone, Apple Watch, powering a wireless charger, etc.
M.2 NVMe SSD
Like the Thunderbolt 4 SuperDock before it, the Echo 21 lets you add up to 8TB of SSD storage via an NVMe M.2 2280 SSD. I added a SanDisk WD_Black SN850X 2TB SSD, which, on paper, is capable of up to 7300 MB/s read, but when used with the Sonnet Echo 21 Thunderbolt 5 SuperDock, speeds max out around 3300 MB/s. This is a major upgrade over the Echo 20, which supports up to 800 MB/s due to its slower Thunderbolt 4 architecture.
While the internal SSD is much faster than it was in the dock’s predecessor, you’ll notice that external Thunderbolt 5 SSDs are faster in both read/write tests. That’s because, in order to properly support 10Gb USB ports and 10GbE, only 2x PCIe lanes were allocated to the internal SSD. The Thunderbolt 5 ports, on the other hand, have access to the full 4x PCIe Gen4 lanes, and thus external Thunderbolt 5 SSDs have more headroom.
Installation of the SSD is dead-simple. At the bottom of the dock, you’ll find the SSD cover plate that can be removed via the two Philips screws. Once the cover is removed, unscrew the standoff screw, insert the SSD, and reinstall the standoff screw to secure the drive.
Once connected to the host computer, macOS will recognize the new SSD. I recommend using Disk Utility to format and manage the new drive.
One of the biggest issues with M.2 drives is that they generate significant heat under sustained load. Sonnet has made a couple of changes to help keep things cool. First, it added a second thermal pad, so now the drive is sandwiched between two pads. Second, and more importantly, it added a fan and corresponding intake port to the ends of the dock.
I will admit, when I first saw the fan, I was concerned. As most of you know, I hate fan noise with a passion, so despite the potential benefits, it initially gave me pause. However, I’m happy to report that the fan noise, while present if you get close enough to the dock, is virtually inaudible at normal distances.
Thunderbolt docks tend to run on the warmer side, and adding an M.2 SSD only increases the thermal footprint. I think adding a fan was a wise decision to help maintain sustained peak drive performance and keep the device cool overall.
Using the Echo 21 Thunderbolt 5 SuperDock
Sonnet’s has long preferred the “flat on the desktop” horizontal approach to dock orientation, and the Echo 21 is no exception. It means the hardware takes up a little more desktop footprint, but enjoys a low center of gravity with cable connections resting close to the desktop surface.
The Echo 21, like its predecessor, features rear-facing Thunderbolt I/O, so there’s no need to permanently connect cables to the front of the dock.
That being said, there are plenty of I/O options within arm’s reach, thanks to eight front-facing ports, including the already-mentioned 15W USB-C port and microSD additions.
Having a much faster internal SSD only adds to the dock’s versatility. You can use it for general storage or for offloading and editing high-resolution, high-frame-rate videos. It’s also a good Time Machine drive candidate, since it’s always connected as long as your Mac is connected to the dock. It’s especially useful for desktop machines like the Mac mini or Mac Studio, which rarely, if ever, leave the desktop.
Display connectivity
If you’re interested in learning which display types the Echo 21 supports with macOS or other platforms, I recommend reading Sonnet’s documentation. Here’s a brief look at how many displays can be configured when connected to the same Mac.
| Display Configuration | Compatible Models | 
|---|---|
| One Display | M1, M2, M3 (1) base models | 
| Two Displays | M4, M5 base models; M1, M2, M3, M4 Pro, and Max models; Intel Macs that support macOS 15+ | 
| Three Displays | M5 Pro and Max models | 
| Four Displays | M5 Max models (requires daisy chain connection of one display) | 
9to5Mac’s Take
The Echo 21 SuperDock and its sister product, the Echo 20 Thunderbolt 5 SecureDock, are both available now. The SecureDock is basically the same dock, except it omits the built-in NVMe SSD option and costs $50 less.
At $499.99, the Sonnet Echo 21 Thunderbolt 5 SuperDock is pricey, but it yields one of the most versatile dock experiences you’ll find. Alongside its versatility, it affords room to grow thanks to the added bandwidth of its Thunderbolt 5 upstream and downstream connectivity. Such connectivity yields immediate benefits – faster I/O with both the internal and externally connected SSDs, and even faster support when you upgrade to a Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac and peripherals.
What do you think about the Echo 21 SuperDock? Is it worth the asking price? Sound off in the comments below with your thoughts.
Jeff’s favorite Mac accessories:
- Whoosh! Screen Cleaner – the best way to clean your Mac’s display
- Asus ProArt 6K Display – the most budget-friendly 6K Display for Mac
- Asus ProArt 5K Display – Pound for pound the best external display for Mac
- Rodecaster Duo – the best and most feature packed audio interface for Mac
- Apple Magic Mouse – the best mouse for Mac, hands-down
articles.summary:
The Sonnet Echo 21 Thunderbolt 5 SuperDock offers high-speed connectivity, 140W power delivery, and an internal M.2 SSD slot to expand the I/O capabilities of modern Mac desktop and laptop computers.

### Key Points
- Features Thunderbolt 5 technology, providing up to 80 Gbps of bidirectional data bandwidth.
- Includes 10Gb Ethernet, SD and microSD UHS-II 4.0 card slots, and high-resolution 24-bit/192 kHz audio support.
- Supports up to three external displays via HDMI, DisplayPort, or Thunderbolt 5 connections.
- Provides 140W of power delivery to the host computer, suitable for high-performance machines like the 16-inch MacBook Pro.
- Includes an internal M.2 NVMe SSD socket for up to 8TB of additional storage with active cooling.
- Available now for $499, offering a significant performance upgrade over the previous Thunderbolt 4 model.

### Why it Matters
This dock provides a future-proof solution for power users who need to maximize the connectivity and storage potential of their Mac workstations. By leveraging Thunderbolt 5, it addresses common bottlenecks in data transfer and display support, making it a versatile tool for professional creative workflows.

articles.title: Apple announces September iPhone launch event
articles.author: Jay Peters
articles.content:
Apple’s next launch event will take place on September 9th at 1PM ET. Invites to the event, which has a “Surprise and shine” tagline, were sent out on Wednesday. The event will take place at the Steve Jobs Theater in Apple Park, but there will also be a livestream on Apple’s website.
Apple announces September iPhone launch event
Apple is gearing up to announce some new gadgets.
Apple is gearing up to announce some new gadgets.
September’s show could be a big one, as Apple may finally announce the long-rumored foldable iPhone. A photo of an apparent dummy unit indicates the foldable may have a wide form factor that’s similar to what Samsung used with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, a phone that our reviewer Dominic Preston said “feels like the future.”
Apple is also expected to refresh its Pro and Pro Max phones, but those are rumored to be iterative upgrades and not a big redesign like Apple announced last year. Should past trends continue, they’ll likely be called the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
However Apple reportedly won’t announce the base model iPhone 18 at the event and instead introduce it next year. In 2027, Apple is also rumored to be launching an iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air.
This event will also be the first with John Ternus as Apple’s CEO. Formerly the company’s hardware chief, Ternus is set to take over from Tim Cook on September 1st.
