Apple will host a product launch event on September 9 at the Steve Jobs Theater, marking the first major presentation under incoming CEO John Ternus.

### Key Points
- The event is scheduled for September 9 at 1:00 PM ET at Apple Park and will be available via livestream.
- Apple may unveil a long-rumored foldable iPhone featuring a wide form factor similar to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold series.
- The company is expected to announce iterative hardware upgrades for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models.
- John Ternus will lead his first major product launch as CEO, officially succeeding Tim Cook on September 1.

### Why it Matters
This event represents a significant leadership transition for Apple as John Ternus takes the helm during a critical period for the company's hardware strategy. The potential introduction of a foldable device could signal a major shift in Apple's competitive positioning within the premium smartphone market.

articles.title: The Meta Settlement Will Put Limits on Instagram for Teens. They’re Still Vulnerable
articles.author: Paresh Dave, Lauren Goode
articles.content:
Advocates for children tell WIRED that Meta’s legal settlement to address concerns about teenagers’ use of social media proposes important and overdue feature changes that invite more parental oversight than ever before. They also, though, say it puts a significant burden on caregivers and unreliable age-assessment systems.
Rather than go through a lengthy federal civil trial—and possible appeals process—in Northern California over the next five weeks, Meta instead on Wednesday agreed to a proposed settlement with a group of state attorneys general, who were suing the social media company for alleged harms against kids on its apps. The settlement includes a payout of up to $16.7 billion overall to states and significant changes to the way Instagram and Facebook work for teen users.
US district judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers approved the settlement on Wednesday.
The settlement fee, paid out in yearly installments over 10 years, would be a rounding error for Meta, which raked in more than $200 billion in revenue last year. Meta shares fared well on Wednesday as investors cheered the pending removal of perhaps the biggest of many teen lawsuits targeting the company.
But the proposed changes to Meta’s flagship apps, which include forced time limits, notification blocks, and a chronological feed option for teens, would be some of the most significant changes Meta has made as a result of the ongoing scrutiny of the company’s policies. California attorney general Rob Bonta called it a “watershed moment.”
Still, child safety advocates and mental health experts doubt the effectiveness of Meta’s proposed changes. Digital rights activists, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, are sounding alarms that the increased age-verification measures that would be built into Meta’s apps for teens would “enshrine Meta's harmful surveillance into law.”
Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment on concerns raised about the settlement.
What’s Changing
In a big win for the states, parents will now be alerted when teens correspond with suspicious accounts or open a second account, sometimes known as a “finsta,” to furtively use Instagram. In addition, parents will receive periodic updates on their children’s use of Instagram and Facebook, including any attempts to evade parental controls.
Very few of the new measures restrict the types of specific content adolescents can see, with the exception of blocking exposure to extreme makeover filters. But there are several new limits on when young users can scroll their feeds. Access will be blocked overnight and will be limited to two hours during the day, unless parents allow more. From August 15 to June 15 each year, during the US school year, notifications will be muted by default from 8 am to 3 pm.
And users may also opt into a non-algorithmic feed and turn off autoplay of videos, though how Meta plans to make those potentially helpful options palatable to teens was unaddressed. Parents, however, can make those settings the default on their children’s accounts.
“These are common-sense regulations that will do a lot of good,” says Jean Twenge, who wrote the book 10 Rules for Raising Kids in a High-Tech World and testified as an expert psychologist for the states during the trial last week. “Teens should not be using social media in the middle of the night, at school, or for so many hours a day that it crowds out time for talking with friends and family, going outside, exercising, and sleeping.”
One of the changes—hiding “like” counts by default—was first tested among a broad set of users about seven years ago. Despite internal research showing that publicly visible “like” counts could contribute to people engaging in harmful social comparison, Meta only rolled out the ability to hide them as an option. “People didn't really go in and adjust those settings in any significant quantities,” Vaishnavi Jayakumar, a former head of youth policy at Meta, said in a deposition last year.
Carol Vidal, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, says the proposed changes are broadly positive. She points specifically to muted notifications at night, for sleep health, and Meta’s proposed limits on plastic surgery filters, noting that “a lot of girls, particularly, are struggling with self-image and comparing themselves online to other people on social media.”
But, Vidal says, measuring the effectiveness of the changes could take years to research.
Why Experts Are Still Concerned
The widespread, immediate responses to Meta’s proposed changes underscore just how complicated it is to regulate social media.
Tanzeem Choudhury, a professor of integrated health and technology at Cornell Tech, the New York City–based research arm of Cornell University, says the proposed changes mostly inject “friction of use.” She points out that measures such as daily limits, nighttime blocks, or muted notifications can be bypassed through secondary accounts or false ages.
So a lot is riding on Meta’s ability to successfully age-gate kids into an experience it calls Teen Accounts. “None of the protections will work if kids and teens can just choose a birth year that makes them 18 or otherwise evade age assurance,” says Twenge, the expert witness.
As part of the deal, Meta agreed to strengthen age assurance but provided few details. “While we'll do all we can to accurately understand someone's age, through both AI prediction technology and steps to confirm someone's age (like ID collection or Yoti's facial scanning), we need app stores to provide us with verified age information from devices,” Meta spokesperson Stephanie Otway says.
Even if successful, age-verification requirements are unwelcome to privacy and security activists. Kate Ruane, the director for the Free Expression Project at the Center for Democracy and Technology, says Meta’s new age assurance tools could pose “significant risks to everyone’s privacy and free-expression rights online.” Electronic Frontier Foundation senior counsel David Greene says that the measures will mean teens have “a lesser ability to exercise their rights to speak, access information and art and culture, associate and form communities, and play.”
Meta also agreed to verify parents more strictly, including limiting the number of accounts each can supervise to hedge against someone running a fake-parent mill. Adam Mosseri, who oversees Instagram for Meta, said on the witness stand this week that at one point less than 1 percent of teens had linked a parent to their account.
It's unclear how Meta will go about significantly boosting that number to get better adoption of its new parental oversight mechanisms. Its proposed system also does not appear to account for parents who are unsupportive of their children, including those who may be gay or lesbian and using social media to find online community. “It could widen existing disparities between children with parents who are actively involved versus those who are less involved or less aware,” Choudhury said.
Meta’s Otway says “the vast majority of the changes in the settlement are on by default, and parents don’t have to do anything” unless they “choose to modify these defaults.” He also notes that teens can set the supervisor of their account to be someone other than their parent, as long as that person is at least 18.
Attorneys for the states acknowledged that there’s no exact solution to improve age-checking or increase parental involvement, but they plan to keep nudging Meta along through an independent auditing team in the years to come.
Others expressed disappointment in the financial penalty, which states had said was not their priority. “It does not come close to accounting for the full scale of harms that Meta has wrought,” said Julie Scelfo, founder of the grassroots group Mothers Against Media Addiction.
Most importantly, the settlement does not by itself bring about a change in Meta’s culture, which former employees testified had stifled their ability to build features to protect teens while at the company. Testimony showed that Meta’s attorneys once scrubbed concerning data about teens on social media from a presentation to leadership. Another team didn’t promote some usage-limit features as much as had been intended, the records showed.
Bonta, the California attorney general, said it is “telling that Meta settled halfway through Mosseri’s testimony and before [CEO] Mark Zuckerberg could take the stand.”
To change Meta’s approach to business, says Arturo Bejar, a former employee who testified last week, the company needs to be held accountable to independently measured reductions in harm to kids. “Under the settlement, Instagram will be used less,” Bejar says, “but will not be safer for young people.”
Update 8/26/26 5:06 pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that the settlement has been accepted by the court.
articles.summary:
Meta has reached a court-approved settlement with state attorneys general to implement significant parental oversight and usage restrictions on Instagram and Facebook to protect teenage users from harm.

### Key Points
- Meta agreed to pay up to $16.7 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits regarding the impact of its platforms on children.
- New features include mandatory daily time limits, overnight access blocks, and muted notifications during school hours for teen accounts.
- Parents will receive alerts regarding suspicious account activity and gain the ability to set default non-algorithmic feeds for their children.
- The settlement requires Meta to strengthen age-verification systems, though critics warn these measures may compromise user privacy and free expression.
- US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers officially approved the settlement, which avoids a lengthy federal civil trial in Northern California.

### Why it Matters
This settlement represents a major regulatory shift in how social media giants manage youth safety, moving toward mandatory friction and parental control features. While the agreement forces Meta to alter its flagship products, experts remain divided on whether these changes will effectively reduce online harm or simply shift the burden of enforcement onto caregivers.

articles.title: I’ve Been a Software Developer For 20 Years. Here’s Why I’m All in on Vibe Coding.
articles.author: Aytekin Tank
articles.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- While vibe coding is exceptional for building a minimum viable product or handling repetitive tasks, you can’t rely on it completely.
- Having a foundational understanding of code matters, even in an era when you don’t always need to write it yourself. The best vibe coding, in my experience, happens when someone who understands the underlying logic is directing the AI — not just accepting whatever it produces.
I’ve been a software developer for so long it’s practically in my bones. Computers have fascinated me since I was a kid, and I built my first web-based business while I was still in college. Jotform, the company I’ve been running for 20 years, started when I grew tired of building tedious web forms by hand at an early job.
Now, vibe coding — using AI to write functional code from plain-language descriptions — has democratized what gets made and who gets to make it. As a programmer, I still think it’s useful to have a fundamental understanding of code. But as a founder, I am thrilled by the possibilities of what vibe coding can do, especially in the early stages of building a startup.
Why? Because now, a good idea can become a reality with far less time and fewer resources. If you’re a green thumb with an incredible new idea for a plant care app, you don’t need to find a co-founder to handle the coding. The same goes for the restaurant owner who wants a custom reservations tool, the consultant who needs a client-facing dashboard or anyone sitting on a great idea who assumed the technical barrier put it out of reach.
Obviously, “vibe coding” was not a phrase that meant anything back in 2006, when my startup began serving its first customers. But if I were starting now, here’s what I’d do.
Building an MVP
In the past, the notion of a minimum viable product, or MVP, was always a little misleading. Even a stripped-down version of an idea required wireframes, a competent developer (yourself or someone else) and a process of tweaking and refining that could take days, if not much, much longer. The idea is that it showcases the core elements of your product, but it doesn’t have to be terribly user-friendly.
Back in college, I spent a long time poring over the MVP for my first early creation, a membership platform called Profile Manager. It worked — and got attention — but frankly, it was clunky. These days, I’d never have to release anything so basic-looking, and even a sleeker version would have taken a fraction of the time to make.
The point of an MVP has always been to gather as much information as possible, as cheaply as possible. Vibe coding doesn’t change that, but it does shorten the space between an idea bouncing around your brain to a genuine prototype you can put out into the world.
Streamlining your day-to-day
When you’re a founder, there are never enough hours in the day. There’s a reason so much ink has been spilled on optimizing, time-maxxing and the importance of squeezing productivity from every spare minute like a piece of citrus fruit into a power smoothie.
Here, vibe coding is also a game-changer. I recently used Claude Code to whip up an app that would supercharge my fitness regimen, acting as both a personal trainer and nutrition coach based on my preferences and behavior. It’s not something I plan to monetize or develop further, but it has helped me dramatically streamline a part of my life, giving me back time to work on other things. Others in my orbit have vibe-coded solutions for tasks like organizing schedules or compiling reports. They don’t need to scale, nor do they need to be perfect — they need only to make one aspect of life a little easier.
Think about the tasks in your week that are genuinely nobody’s job. These are perfect candidates for a vibe-coded solution. If something costs you time every week, and you can describe what a better version would look like, you can probably build it.
What it all means
Whether you’re using Claude Code, Lovable or Base44, all vibe coding tools offer the promise of the same thing: a world where what you can build is restricted only by your imagination. That said, vibe coding has its limits, and it’s important to understand what they are.
First, while vibe coding is exceptional for building an MVP or handling repetitive tasks, you can’t rely on it completely. Around 45% of AI-generated code has security weaknesses — according to Daily.dev, a security scan of 1,645 web apps built using Lovable revealed that 120 of them exposed users’ personal data due to critical vulnerabilities. The fact is, tasks like authentication, payment processing and encryption still demand human expertise that AI models can’t reliably provide.
This is why I still believe a foundational understanding of code matters, even in an era when you don’t always need to write it yourself. The best vibe coding, in my experience, happens when someone who understands the underlying logic is directing the AI — not just accepting whatever it produces.
When used with the proper foreknowledge and precautions, vibe coding is a game-changer for even tech-savvy entrepreneurs. Use it to create your first MVP and streamline your operations, and unlock valuable hours that will add up significantly.
Key Takeaways
- While vibe coding is exceptional for building a minimum viable product or handling repetitive tasks, you can’t rely on it completely.
- Having a foundational understanding of code matters, even in an era when you don’t always need to write it yourself. The best vibe coding, in my experience, happens when someone who understands the underlying logic is directing the AI — not just accepting whatever it produces.
I’ve been a software developer for so long it’s practically in my bones. Computers have fascinated me since I was a kid, and I built my first web-based business while I was still in college. Jotform, the company I’ve been running for 20 years, started when I grew tired of building tedious web forms by hand at an early job.
Now, vibe coding — using AI to write functional code from plain-language descriptions — has democratized what gets made and who gets to make it. As a programmer, I still think it’s useful to have a fundamental understanding of code. But as a founder, I am thrilled by the possibilities of what vibe coding can do, especially in the early stages of building a startup.
Why? Because now, a good idea can become a reality with far less time and fewer resources. If you’re a green thumb with an incredible new idea for a plant care app, you don’t need to find a co-founder to handle the coding. The same goes for the restaurant owner who wants a custom reservations tool, the consultant who needs a client-facing dashboard or anyone sitting on a great idea who assumed the technical barrier put it out of reach.

articles.title: NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA) & Blackstone (BX): Nvidia Wants Wall Street to Lend Against AI Chips Like They’re Mortgages
articles.author: Fatima Gulzar
articles.content:
NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA) & Blackstone (BX): Nvidia Wants Wall Street to Lend Against AI Chips Like They’re Mortgages
NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) is trying to turn its AI chips into an entirely new asset class. The company announced partnerships with six major financial firms, Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR, to launch "compute financing platforms" aimed at raising more than $500 billion in outside capital for AI infrastructure. CEO Jensen Huang said Nvidia could backstop up to $125 billion, or 25%, of the potential deals.
Blackstone Inc. (NYSE:BX) President Jon Gray said on CNBC that AI compute will be seen as a "financeable asset class," much like how mortgage lenders assess homes.
Why This Matters
Nvidia is trying to make Wall Street treat AI chips as bankable infrastructure right as skepticism about AI spending is rising.
That leaves a real tension: is this smart financial engineering that unlocks the AI buildout, or a sign the industry needs increasingly creative ways to keep the spending machine running?
The Bull and Bear Case: Nvidia
CEO Huang argues that because NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)'s hardware is broadly used and transferable across customers, lenders can reliably treat compute as a long-lived and revenue-generating asset rather than rapidly depreciating equipment. Nvidia widens the pool of buyers who can afford its chips without footing most of the capital bill itself by helping customers finance purchases off their own balance sheets. The move follows Nvidia's existing SK Hynix memory partnership and a reported deal to guarantee financing for a 10-gigawatt Ohio data center leased to OpenAI. It is part of a broader pattern of Nvidia actively engineering both supply and demand at once.
However, commentators, including an FT column, have flagged "circular financing" concerns, the risk that Nvidia is effectively financing its own demand, which could obscure how healthy the underlying AI economics really are. NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) shares actually fell after the deal was first reported, erasing more than $70 billion in market value, suggesting some investors read it skeptically rather than as good news outright. The announcement also comes weeks after a July market swoon in which investors openly questioned whether trillions in AI capital spending will ever pay off, and after Moody's warned that heavy capex is squeezing free cash flow and pushing tech giants toward more debt.
The Bull and Bear Case: Blackstone
Blackstone Inc. (NYSE:BX) gets a front-row seat to structuring what its president calls a new financeable asset class at a moment when AI compute demand across Blackstone's portfolio companies has already surged sevenfold this year. The firm has prior experience financing AI infrastructure for companies like Anthropic. This gives it a head start in building similar Nvidia-backed products. Blackstone joined a $500 billion project as one of only six partners. The company plans to invest a huge amount of money into the effort. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink compared this moment to the creation of mortgage-backed investments back in the 1970s.
articles.summary:
Nvidia is partnering with six major financial firms, including Blackstone and Goldman Sachs, to launch a $500 billion financing platform that treats AI chips as bankable infrastructure assets.

### Key Points
- Nvidia aims to raise $500 billion in outside capital to fund AI infrastructure, with the company pledging to backstop up to $125 billion of the total deals.
- The initiative involves partnerships with Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to create new compute financing platforms.
- Blackstone President Jon Gray stated that AI compute is being positioned as a financeable asset class, drawing comparisons to the structure of mortgage-backed securities.
- Nvidia’s strategy allows customers to finance hardware purchases off their own balance sheets, potentially widening the buyer pool for its high-end AI chips.
- Skeptics have raised concerns regarding "circular financing," questioning whether the move obscures the underlying health of AI demand and capital spending.

### Why it Matters
This initiative attempts to normalize AI hardware as a long-term, revenue-generating asset to sustain massive industry spending despite growing investor skepticism. By engineering new financial structures, Nvidia seeks to ensure continued demand for its chips while shifting the capital burden away from its own balance sheet.

articles.title: Crypto bro faces 280 years in prison for defrauding investors with promises of an 'AI supercomputer' for mining — jury convicts businessman of running $24-million Ponzi scheme, claimed up to 30% APR and a 100% money-back guarantee
articles.author: editors@tomshardware.com (Jowi Morales) , Jowi Morales
articles.content:
A Nevada court has found a Las Vegas businessman guilty of 11 counts of wire fraud, two counts of mail fraud, and two counts of money laundering for defrauding over $24 million from hundreds of investors. According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Brent Kovar presented Profit Connect to investors as a crypto mining operation that used an artificial intelligence supercomputer for its operations. He promised a fixed rate of return that paid 15% to 30% APR and also came with a 100% money-back guarantee. However, it turned out that the “profits” that the earlier investors made only came from the influx of newer investors, and that the company wasn’t making any money.
Kovar victimized 400 investors, telling them that the company had cryptocurrency reserves worth hundreds of millions of dollars. In reality, it had zero holdings, couldn’t afford to pay investors their interest earnings, and had no way to return their cash despite the offered guarantee. “He used investor money to operate Profit Connect, to buy gifts for employees, to buy a house for himself, and to repay investors as if those repayments came from mining cryptocurrency and verifying cryptocurrency transactions,” the Department of Justice said in its press release.
Profit Connect operated from 2017 to 2021, which is around the same time that Bitcoin made its first major rally, with the cryptocurrency hitting a peak of over $19,000 in December of that year. This, combined with the buzzwords of “AI” and “supercomputer,” made it seem to investors that they were putting money in a groundbreaking new technology that would change the way we do finance. Unfortunately, the venture turned out to be a scam and defrauded investors out of their money with nothing to show for. It’s unclear if the funds that the investors lost will ever be recovered, but Kovar is facing a possibly lengthy jail time of a maximum of 280 years for his crimes.
Another scam rooted in cryptocurrency investment from 2017 saw retail investors lose $2 billion. BitConnect offered a similar guaranteed return on investment for anyone who put up cash on its platform until 2018, but instead of using the deposited money for trading, it was just siphoned off to the organization’s private digital wallet addresses. Even before this, another Ponzi-scheme scammer made off with $6 billion from her victims in China from 2014 until 2017 and converted it into 61,000 Bitcoin. While she has already been arrested, the seized cryptocurrency is still in limbo, so it’s unclear if and when her victims will get their money back.

### Key Points

- The Profit Connect scheme defrauded approximately 400 investors of $24 million between 2017 and 2021.

- Evidence revealed the company held zero cryptocurrency reserves and used new investor funds to pay earlier participants and personal expenses.

### Why it Matters
This case highlights the ongoing risks associated with investment schemes that leverage buzzwords like artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency to exploit retail investors. It serves as a stark reminder of the importance of due diligence, as victims of such Ponzi schemes often face significant challenges in recovering lost capital.

Motorola shares all the new features coming with its Android 17 update
Aug 26, 2026 — 9:37 AM ET
- Motorola has shared the official changelog for its Android 17 update.
- Updates include a refreshed Quick Settings panel, stackable widgets, cross-platform Quick Share, enhanced HDR brightness control, and more.
Motorola’s stable Android 17 update rollout is underway this month, starting with its flagship Signature series. While we previously tracked the eligible devices lineup and previewed early changes during the Android 17 beta cycle, this marks the first time we’ve gained access to the official changelog for the stable Android 17 update reaching Motorola devices.
According to a report by FoneArena, Motorola’s Android 17 update brings a refreshed system UI, an upgraded Quick Settings menu, expanded cross-platform file sharing, device diagnostics, and new AI and anti-scam security protections. This is the official changelog shared by the report:
- Interface and Usability Updates
  - System Layout: The update introduces a refreshed Quick Settings panel and redesigned system menus featuring larger touch targets and streamlined navigation.
  - Display and Personalization: The home screen interface has been updated alongside refined display settings, including enhanced HDR brightness management.
  - Widgets: Interactive widgets now support snap-scrolling functionality for smoother browsing within smaller screen footprints.
  - Accessibility: Vision settings, display scaling, and screen magnification have received structural updates to simplify control adjustments.
- Connectivity and Device Management
  - Cross-Platform Quick Share: File sharing now supports cross-ecosystem transfers via Quick Share QR codes, enabling non-Android and iOS users to download shared media through a web interface.
  - Network & Audio Sharing: Added tools include Instant Hotspot for seamless tethering setup and Nearby Audio Streams to broadcast audio to adjacent compatible receivers.
  - Hardware Diagnostics: A built-in device diagnostics hub allows users to evaluate individual hardware component health and review system telemetry locally.
- Intelligence, Privacy, and Security
  - AI-Powered Circle to Search: The visual lookup tool now includes real-time, on-screen language translation directly within the interface.
  - Scam Protection: An automated scam detection system scans incoming SMS, MMS, and RCS messages to alert users to potential phishing attempts.
  - Security Locks: Android 17 incorporates a Failed Authentication Lock alongside strengthened PIN protocols and restricted visibility for sensitive notifications on lock screens.
  - Notification Management: Expanded notification grouping algorithms provide summarized alerts and contextual sharing nudges for newly captured media.
Documentation on Motorola’s support portal gives us another changelog for the stable Android 17 update. However, this changelog appears to pertain to the broader platform-related features that are generally available in Android 17 rather than the unique features coming to Motorola’s UX skin:
- Home screen and quick settings improvements
  - Stackable widgets
    - You can now stack widgets, combining multiple widgets into a single block on your home screen.
    - Instead of taking up several grids on your home screen for your weather, calendar, battery and music player, stack them and swipe the stack to switch between them.
  - Themed icons
    - You can now use an icon theme that coordinates with your overall theme. Touch & hold a blank space on your Home screen, then tap Home settings > Themed icons.
  - Hide quick setting labels when using Classic style
    - If you’re using Classic style for quick settings, you can now hide labels on the settings tiles. Hiding them frees up screen space if you already recognise the icons.
- Stackable widgets
- Improved notifications
  - Live updates
    - Live updates let apps to display real-time, ongoing data. Instead of sending multiple notifications, an app can now continuously update a single live snippet in your status bar or notifications. You can turn these on or off.
  - Notification summaries
    - You can now peek at your notifications for a one-sentence summary of a lengthy group chat or a rapid-fire thread from messaging apps (like WhatsApp or Messages).
  - Organised notifications
    - Your phone now organises your notifications to separate your personal messages from clutter and automated alerts. It uses machine learning to screen lower-priority notifications and bundles them into separate, quiet folders under the Silent section of your notifications.
- Live updates
- New settings
  - Enhanced HDR brightness control
    - When you view HDR content – like an Ultra HDR photo in Google Photos, a HDR video on YouTube or an HDR feed on Instagram – your phone’s display automatically sets brightness to its highest limits to make the highlights pop.
    - You can now limit this brightness to a more comfortable level by adjusting the intensity of Enhanced HDR brightness or turning it off to force HDR photos and videos to play at a normal brightness level.
  - New sharing features in Connected devices
    - There are two new ways to share in Settings > Connected devices:
      - To share a photo or file with one other person, use Tap to Share by placing your phones together.
      - To share with a reusable group, use Quick Drop to send photos or files to friends or a team simultaneously.
  - There are two new ways to share in Settings > Connected devices:
- Enhanced HDR brightness control
- Other improvements: Android system upgrades add more than new features. Using the latest Android update provides other improvements, such as:
  - Enhanced security and protection to defend against evolving threats like malware, phishing and data breaches
  - App compatibility with newer apps, which often require the latest Android version to function correctly
  - Performance improvements that optimise your phone’s operating system for smoother performance, better stability and, in some cases, longer battery life
  - Bug fixes and stability enhancements to resolve known issues and improve overall reliability and stability
While seeing the official changelogs provides welcome clarity on what Android 17 brings to Motorola devices, the broader rollout picture remains somewhat murky. Motorola’s official eligibility list has been riddled with several baffling inconsistencies, from listing unannounced models like the Edge 70 Neo and Edge 70 Plus to duplicate entries for the Edge 60. More concerning is that several relatively recent devices with active update commitments, including the Edge 50 series, Edge 60 Neo, Razr 2024, and Moto G75, were curiously left off the official roster.
Given Motorola’s historically spotty track record with software update commitments and even communication, we hope the company resolves these discrepancies and clarifies whether the omitted handsets will eventually join the Android 17 queue.

articles.title: AurionMail: E2EE suite (CryptPad/Stalwart) with single-password UX
articles.author: AurionMail
articles.content:
TL;DR: AurionMail Suite delivers a Proton-like user experience by combining proven technologies such as CryptPad, Bulwark Webmail, Stalwart Mail Server, Ory Hydra, and OpenPGP.
CryptPad is a powerful collaborative suite, but email falls outside its core scope. Consequently, using encrypted documents alongside encrypted emails traditionally requires managing two separate accounts and passwords.
AurionMail acts as the orchestrator linking CryptPad and a JMAP-based email service into a single, unified workflow.
Users only need to remember one single password to encrypt and decrypt both their emails and CryptPad documents. You enter it once per session to access CryptPad, the webmail, or both.
Additionally, we refreshed CryptPad's UI to provide a modern, cohesive look and feel across the suite.
Demonstrate the Single login to access Mail encryption and Cryptpad documents + the new Cryptpad UI
Existing privacy solutions usually force a compromise between user experience, self-hosting control, and open standards.
Commercial suites offer a seamless single-password workflow, but their backends remain closed-source. On the other hand, self-hosted alternatives often fragment the user experience, requiring users to manage separate accounts and passwords for email and document collaboration.
AurionMail Suite bridges this gap by delivering the smooth Zero-Knowledge experience of commercial platforms on top of a 100% open-source, standards-compliant, self-hosted stack.
| Feature | Proton Suite | Nextcloud + Mail | Standard CryptPad | AurionMail Suite | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100% Open Source & Self-Hosted | ❌ (Proprietary backend) | 🟢 Yes | 🟢 Yes | 🟢 Yes | 
| E2EE Email & Documents | 🟢 Yes | 🟡 (Complex / Plugin-based) | ❌ (No built-in email) | 🟢 Yes | 
| Unified Identity & Encryption (1 Password) | 🟢 Yes | ❌ (Fragmented SSO / Manual PGP) | ❌ (Docs-only account scope) | 🟢 Yes | 
| Open Standards (OpenPGP, JMAP) | 🟡 (OpenPGP supported, limited key discovery) | 🟢 Yes | ❌ (N/A for email) | 🟢 Yes | 
CryptPad excels at secure document collaboration but lacks email. AurionMail extends CryptPad with a fully integrated, E2EE JMAP email client—sharing the same single Zero-Knowledge password so users don't have to manage two isolated systems.
Nextcloud Mail is a standard IMAP client that relies on browser extensions (like Mailvelope) and manual PGP key management for end-to-end encryption. AurionMail delivers seamless, out-of-the-box Zero-Knowledge encryption without complex user workflows.
Proton offers a smooth single-password experience, but its backend is closed-source and locks you into their cloud. AurionMail gives you that exact same seamless user experience on a 100% open-source, self-hosted stack built on open standards.
- Single Password Encryption: Authenticate and encrypt all user data with one master password.
- Single Logout: Logging out from either Webmail or CryptPad automatically logs you out across the entire session/device.
- Global Logout ("Logout from all devices").
- Password change Change your master password without loosing your data.
- Key Synchronization: Seamless key syncing across authorized user devices.
- Core Integrations: Full feature sets inherited from underlying services (CryptPad, Bulwark Webmail and the PGP E2E Plugin for Bulwark).
- Account install : You can create users in LDAP with your workflow and give them a temporary password. Users then visit sso.domain/init to create their master password and activate their account.
- Web Key Server : Imported/Generated key in the PGP Plugin are automatically discoverable with Web Key Directory.
- Emergency Account Hold: A secure URL generated at account creation that disables the account if accessed (protecting data if a master password is compromised).
- Emergency Account Destruction: A secure URL that permanently destroys the account and its associated keys if visited.
| Login – Login page. | Logout – Logout page. | 
| Bulwark's Aurion Plugin – Manage keys, change password, with the Aurion Plugin. | Email Encryption – Send encryptped emails to your contacts. | 
| Cryptpad Drive – Cryptpad is integrated with a refreshed and modern UI | Cryptpad Settings – You can still edit your cryptpad settings. | 
Here is how the components fit together. Items highlighted in bold are built by the Aurion team:
- LDAP: User management (Identity Source of Truth).
- Ory Hydra: SSO OAuth2/OIDC backend handling authorization flows.
- SSO Web App: Frontend for authentication and Zero-Knowledge key derivation.
- Stalwart Server: High-performance JMAP mail server backend.
- Bulwark Webmail: Webmail frontend interface.
- Bulwark PGP Plugin: Extension enabling end-to-end OpenPGP mail encryption.
- Core-API: Central server managing key sync, session state, and inter-app communication.
- Bridges: Lightweight bridge scripts handling secure secret sharing during login/logout routines.
- CryptPad (Customized): Integrated with the SSO plugin and custom styling for a unified UI.
AurionMail is a distributed suite. However, you can use Orchestra to get a single binary covering
- Hydra
- SSO
- Bulwark
- Core API
- Bridges
- Cryptpad Customized
See Installation Guide for more details.

The new AurionMail Suite integrates CryptPad and JMAP-based email into a single, open-source platform that uses one master password for unified, end-to-end encrypted document and email management.

### Key Points
- AurionMail combines CryptPad, Bulwark Webmail, Stalwart Mail Server, and Ory Hydra into a cohesive, self-hosted suite.
- The platform enables a Zero-Knowledge experience where one password manages both email encryption and collaborative document access.
- It utilizes open standards including OpenPGP and JMAP to ensure interoperability without relying on proprietary backends.

- Administrators can deploy the suite via the Orchestra binary, which bundles all core services and custom integrations into a single package.

AurionMail bridges the gap between the convenience of commercial platforms like Proton and the transparency of self-hosted, open-source software. By eliminating the need for fragmented logins and manual PGP key management, it provides a professional-grade privacy solution for users who require full control over their data infrastructure.

articles.title: ROOKE: Big Tech Broke The Social Contract And American Workers Haven’t Forgotten
articles.author: Mary Rooke
articles.content:
At the heart of the legal immigration debate is a broken social contract between Silicon Valley and the middle class.
Americans have become increasingly frustrated with the wave of legal immigration brought into the U.S. to replace American workers. This primarily started in the tech industry, where the pipeline for middle-class Americans to access the American Dream was first removed.
Americans designed and built the first personal computers in the 70s and 80s. By 1993, Mosaic rolled out its internet browser for Windows and Macintosh, connecting the world to the internet. Americans had successfully created the tech boom that hasn’t slowed down since. Middle-class Americans thought this line of work would be the wave of the future. They pushed their children into tech specialties, telling them that if they worked hard, they could be the next generation of innovators.
This was the unwritten contract. Our children would focus less on economics, medicine, and other specialties, with the promise that the tech industry would fulfill its end by hiring them upon graduation. Sadly, the U.S. Congress passed the Immigration Act of 1990, creating an annual 65,000 visa cap allowing foreign workers to replace the middle class.
Palmer Luckey, Oculus founder and Anduril CEO, claimed to have observed H-1B visa abuse in Silicon Valley, calling it a scam that replaces U.S. workers with foreign labor, during an interview on the Shawn Ryan Show in February 2025.
“Of course there is so much H-1B abuse. You would not believe what I saw when I was in Silicon Valley. It is insane. It’s obviously a program to replace U.S. workers with, basically, slave labor that can’t ever escape,” he said.
Computer-related occupations accounted for only 26 percent of H-1Bs in 1995 but almost doubled to 42 percent in 1996, according to a Center for Migration Studies paper published in the Sage Journal.
The demand for foreign labor wasn’t spontaneously created by Congress. The information and communications technology industry (ICT) lobbied for it.
“The ICT industry has been the dominant user of the H-1B program over the past two decades,” the paper stated. “The major source of these workers in turn has been India. In 2000, 49 percent of all approved H-1B petitions were for Indian citizens, and by 2015, that figure had increased to 71 percent.” (Sign up for Mary Rooke’s weekly newsletter here!)
Everyone from Microsoft, Google, Cisco, Facebook (now META), Oracle, Intel, and Qualcomm employed substantial numbers of H-1B workers. And they wanted more.
“ICT firms began to use the program heavily, and the annual limit became a constraint. Starting in the mid-1990s, therefore, ICT firms began working to raise the H-1B cap. Harris Miller, a professional lobbyist with expertise in immigration, was hired as president of the Information Technology Association of America (ITAA) in 1995. A new business association, American Business for Legal Immigration (ABLI), was established with financial support from prominent ICT firms and designed to focus specifically on skilled immigration,” the paper stated.
Former President Bill Clinton and the Democratic Party solicited help from ICT firms for his 1996 reelection campaign. At the time, there weren’t any anti-immigration organizations large enough to fight back against the growing access the tech industry had to the federal government through its political action committee, TechNet. This wasn’t just a Democratic Party issue. Republicans are just as much to blame.
By the early 2000s, Americans were being replaced en masse, and ICT lobbying firms continued their march to raise the cap on how many foreign workers could be granted U.S. visas.
In just 33 years, the U.S. tech industry went from using raw American talent to build the internet to casting them aside in favor of cheaper foreign labor.
Isaiah Taylor, founder of Valar Atomics, opined on the increasingly hostile relationship between Americans and tech, arguing that a middle ground must be found before it’s too late.
“Tech bros need to remember that they exist within a nation that has a people, not a blank economic zone,” Taylor wrote. “Middle class America needs to remember that national strength comes from economic and technological strength.”
“This is a careful synthesis between these that we must strike,” he added.
Tech bros need to remember that they exist within a nation that has a people, not a blank economic zone
Middle class America needs to remember that national strength comes from economic and technological strength
This is a careful synthesis between these that we must strike
But he’s missing a very important fact here. It wasn’t the middle class that broke the social contract. The tech industry, with its greed and clear lack of loyalty to Americans who made it, did. The middle class was more than happy to continue bolstering the tech industry. It was excited about the advancements in technology, and especially about being a part of its rise. However, what Taylor and the rest of the “tech bros” are asking is that Americans ignore the betrayal and support it anyway. They want the middle class to continue to lose out to foreign workers without complaint. But that just isn’t going to happen anymore. (ROOKE: Trump Administration Takes Big Bite Of Immigration Apple With $103,265 Fee)
If the tech industry is worried about how the growing discontent among Americans will affect its ability to grow, then it needs to take a clear-eyed look at what caused the divide. The success of data centers, social media, and AI all revolves around their desire to fix the relationship between tech and the middle class. Any call to action should start with a renewed social contract. One that benefits American workers and doesn’t leave them training their replacements.
Follow Mary Rooke on X: @MaryRooke
articles.summary:
Silicon Valley faces growing scrutiny over the H-1B visa program, as critics argue that tech companies have systematically replaced American workers with cheaper foreign labor since 1990.

### Key Points
- The Immigration Act of 1990 established a 65,000 annual visa cap, which the information and communications technology industry lobbied to increase.
- By 2015, Indian citizens accounted for 71 percent of all approved H-1B petitions, up from 49 percent in 2000.
- Major tech firms including Microsoft, Google, Meta, Intel, and Qualcomm have been identified as significant users of the H-1B program.
- Oculus founder Palmer Luckey publicly criticized the H-1B system in February 2025, labeling it a mechanism for replacing U.S. workers with foreign labor.
- Research indicates that computer-related occupations grew from 26 percent of H-1B visas in 1995 to 42 percent by 1996.

### Why it Matters
The debate highlights a deepening rift between the domestic workforce and the tech sector regarding the future of American employment. If this tension remains unresolved, it could lead to significant regulatory shifts or political pressure aimed at restricting foreign labor access for major technology companies.

articles.title: It's so hard to finish an idea that is not yours (and suggested by AI)
articles.author: Simon Späti
articles.content:
Keep AI Out of Your (Obsidian) Vault
Everyone is using Obsidian for AI, or wants to use it to become more productive. But I think it’s a dead end.
The reasons are clear: Obsidian notes are open on your local disk in an open format, Markdown, and accessible to everyone, including your AI agents. This makes it as great and easy an integration as possible. But should you actually use AI with your notes? And if so, what are the use cases or ways you should interact with it?
First of all, if you use Vibe Code Agents with Obsidian, use the Obsidian CLI. It will be much faster to return your files, search, or act, grepping through the files.
Second, I’m a strong proponent of avoiding adding lots of AI-generated summaries[^1] or other on-the-fly-generated text to my vault. The reason is simple: over time, I don’t know anymore whether the content was written by me or by an AI, and my own, much more valuable thoughts get diminished by “AI Slop”.
- Also, when searching for something, you need to fight through the noise of generated stuff. If you only have your own writing, it’s all valuable, or at least there’s a reason why you noted it down. There was a conviction, idea, or something that moved you.
- Yes, it’s good in certain areas, and mostly on-the-spot summaries seem great, but every time I come back to them, I find them very average. It doesn’t help me, as it didn’t highlight the things I would, and I need to reread anyway.
- What I do sometimes with Obsidian Webclipper, if I create a new note, is summarize it in one sentence or a few. I clearly mark it as AI-generated and even put it in a quote, so it’s clear to me, and to anyone in 5 years, that it wasn’t mine. If I have added my own thoughts and writing, I will just remove the generated paragraphs (not my words).
But, use it for advanced research, like finding related notes. I think this might be the best use case. But don’t use it for tagging or organization, because eventually all your relations and connections won’t count for anything, since they aren’t made by you. The power lies in the deliberately created graph of notes, your very own Second Brain.
My Obsidian Vault with Smart Lookup and related notes with Smart Connections and local graph | Also check out Vim Motions for Writers to see my writing workflow and how I write
I personally don’t use it like that yet, but I might one day with a powerful local model, since I have lots of sensitive notes I don’t want to upload anywhere. Plus, it takes away the thinking part of My Obsidian Note-Taking Workflow. I don’t want to replace my human thinking yet. But I use a mathematical or local model with Obsidian Smart Connections, or the Graph Analysis plugin.
I’m pretty sure that if you go all in with using AI to generate your notes, you will end up with less clarity and fewer insights. You might start fresh very soon, as you won’t get value from it, and stop maintaining or adding ideas.
[^1] To be clear, I mean long summaries, no harm in a 1-2 sentence intro in a note.
Long AI Summarization is usually just noise
Kepano says, too: “A summary of a PDF is noise. An insight I had from reading the PDF is signal”. Tweet. Read more Other Opinions by Jason Fried, Paul Graham, Ted Gioia, Mitchell Hashimoto, and many more.
# Search is an Organizational Question
I think if you have an urge to do something, do it in a separate vault, or just use a database, e.g. DuckDB, and do all the fun stuff with AI as I did for search and clustering. But don’t mix your precious notes and Zettelkasten for it. Not yet, at least, but probably never.
I have 25'979 files totaling 3.5 GB, all in a single vault, and I find everything in split seconds (using the Omnisearch plugin). Search is pretty much an organizational question; e.g., I use Zettelkasten, and some refer to Memex as its digital version.
But if you need more advanced features, you can just add the Obsidian Smart Connections plugin and get vector and similarity search, etc., out of the box.
# Your Notes Will Be Your Prompts Tomorrow
Remember, your notes will be prompts or libraries for AI tomorrow, but not if you generate them.
# Cultivating Knowledge
Also on the notion of cultivating knowledge for AI systems, I’d say I’m more interested in cultivating for myself, long-term 🙂.
I imagine if humans do not have their own knowledge bases, everyone will have the same (average) notes based on AI models, not 100% of course, but there is no conviction, no decisions made, just all equally similar.
This is another reason we also need human-curated knowledge on a large scale. AI models will retrain on this data, better than on synthetic, fake data, IMO, though we need to find an economic model that also works for the creator of these insights and knowledge.
# Whose Knowledge System is It?
Using Claude Code (or another agent) to generate your system and make connections, like , is not your system. If you want a tool for retrieval, yes, sure, but I have a second brain and a knowledge system where my thinking happens. I make the connections because I had an idea, or something told me to do so.
Great video on this with more of the same thinking I have at Obsidian vs Claude — Why I’m Not Worried About AI Killing Note-Taking Apps. He says elegantly that a second brain is a system; the connections and writing parts are not inefficient; it’s the process of thinking and learning.
Claude is just a tool, like Obsidian, but as File Over App, by the CEO of Obsidian, goes, it’s not about the app anyway, it’s about the files, your thoughts, your insights. So if it’s someone else’s, heck, even generated, it’s not why I use the second brain. Can be useful, too, sure, but not as much as my new ideas, the thinking I get from my knowledge system.
Touch some grass, they say.
# Examples
Some examples that identify this phenomenon quite well, or help us understand and think through it better.
# It’s Hard to Finish an Idea that is not Yours
While I use Claude a lot for my Omarchy plugins and Linux optimization/failure detection, I don’t use it for writing and note-taking, especially for coming up with unique ideas and driving them home by writing them through to the end.
It’s so hard to finish an idea that is not yours and is just suggested by AI.
# Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Knowledge
Andrej Karpathy LLM Knowledge Auto Research, which is another good example of how not to do it (IMO), especially if you like to learn. Sure, it’s fun and helpful, but it will lose its appeal and value over time. It’s like this Reddit quote says it well:
I definitely agree that the ‘Karpathy LLM Wiki’ mediated knowledge base everyone is excited about is not a useful way to actually learn or manage your learned and curated data for the reasons written. If instead you do just want an automated research summary of some knowledge - sure why not, but it’s not particularly interesting and I really don’t get the excitement about it. Reddit
Some great discussion in this thread on this topic.
# Does not Scale, or Will Die Very soon
Automating the links and connections like this won’t sustain for YOUR second brain, for your ideas and notes - you are skipping the thinking, and IMO, the insights. Most of my ideas come from linking and seeing the links I made myself, sometimes years back.
A good example of what not to do for your own vault. 
Tweet
For sure interesting to see what comes out, but I wouldn’t recommend it for your “second brain” where you develop your thinking and YOUR ideas.
If you want the above brain, which is not yours, you should use Wikipedia. Wikipedia graphs and wikilinks give you great insights, as the automated AI ones (probably more), but made by human collaborators. But if you want to create your own knowledge base, I’d do it manually. The payoff comes over the year, it compounds.
# PARA Method: Dedicated Folder
The PARA method by Tiago Forte is super convenient - and you could create an AI folder in resources and put all generated notes there and hide that from search or through other mechanisms. This way, you could still have AI-generated insights or notes that you can link, if helpful, to your original notes.
# Voice to Text
AI with Voice to Text can be another approach to use with Obsidian, which makes sense when you are in a car or so.
But because of my talking much more compared to when I write, and to AI or translator service not understanding all my words, it’s much more work for me than just typing it out. Plus, I usually skip the thinking, though sometimes talking it through can add to the process.
# Slowing Down: Have More Impact Long-term?
See Slowing Down.
# Creativity by Its Very Nature is Forward-looking
# Further Reads

References: Writing is Thinking!,
articles.summary:
Integrating artificial intelligence into personal note-taking systems like Obsidian risks diluting original insights and diminishing the cognitive benefits of the deliberate, human-led process of building a "second brain."

### Key Points
- Avoid cluttering personal vaults with AI-generated summaries, which can obscure original thoughts and create "AI slop" that hinders long-term knowledge retrieval.
- Use AI tools sparingly for specific tasks like finding related notes or performing vector searches, rather than for automated tagging or organizational connections.
- Maintain a clear distinction between human-authored content and AI-generated text by using quotes or separate folders, such as a dedicated resource folder under the PARA method.
- Prioritize manual note-taking and link creation, as the process of connecting ideas is essential for deep learning and developing unique, long-term insights.
- Leverage local plugins like Obsidian Smart Connections or Omnisearch to maintain privacy and efficiency without relying on external AI models for core thinking.

### Why it Matters
Over-reliance on AI to generate or organize personal knowledge bases threatens to replace the critical thinking process that defines a true "second brain." By prioritizing human-curated content, users ensure their notes remain a valuable, authentic repository of personal conviction rather than a collection of generic, machine-generated data.

articles.title: I ditched my travel laptop for a mini PC with a 100-inch screen
articles.author: Chandraveer Mathur
articles.content:
I have a love-hate relationship with my old laptop. It's a nearly decade-old 16-inch HP Pavilion that's still large by today's standards. However, the screen size pales when compared to the 32-inch 1440p panel on my desktop. My laptop is also really heavy for the performance it offers, and an outstation trip last year reminded me why it's better off gathering dust at home. On the flip side, I don't travel nearly enough to justify replacing the laptop with yet another 16-incher just for improved performance and a lighter carry-on bag.
That logic held up until a recent camping trip, where I tried an unconventional arrangement since my Xgimi Mogo 3 Pro portable projector was coming along. I added a Khadas Mind mini PC and wireless peripherals for computing, with a Satechi 4-port GaN travel charger to power it all. Unorthodox as it may be, I'm convinced this is the upgrade I needed.
A projector is the ultimate travel monitor
And entertainment center
My primary annoyance is split-screen multitasking on laptops is plagued by readability and scaling issues. The portable projector has a 1080p native resolution, integrated speakers, Android TV OS, and a tripod base with batteries that last an hour. With mini HDMI input, I can project on any hotel room wall and enjoy a 40 to 100-inch screen. Sure, color accuracy suffers with ambient light, but multitasking and readability aren't an issue anymore. The greater viewing distance and non-emissive display tech add an element of comfort too.
Moreover, the smart projector eliminates the frustrations of setting up, with automatic keystone, focus, obstacle avoidance, and wall color compensation. The ¼-inch thread in the base attaches securely to my camera tripod if the projector isn't perched on the nightstand. These conveniences make the larger display an upgrade more than a tradeoff. When the PC is disconnected, the projector also doubles up as an entertainment hub with the usual Android TV apps.
A mini PC for the horsepower
Powered by a travel charger
My Khadas Mind is the heart of this mobile computing experience, packing a 13th-gen Intel Core i7 notebook processor and 32GB of RAM. The performance upgrade from my Pavilion is staggering — dozens of browser tabs, background tasks, and participating in meetings don't even sweat it. Importantly, this contemporary notebook horsepower fits in a footprint barely larger than a passport. Despite its compact size, the mini PC doesn't skimp on connectivity, offering a full suite of USB, Thunderbolt, and HDMI to connect peripherals and the projector easily.
Before traveling, some paper napkin math confirmed the Khadas' peak power draw was well within the Satechi GaN travel charger's spec, even while it powered the projector through another output. This multi-port charger with swappable international pins can power my wonky workstation from just a single outlet, just like a laptop. For I/O, I threw in a basic Logitech wireless keyboard-mouse combo with the brand's Unifying Receiver tech, so I still have one USB-A and USB-C port free on the Khadas. I could go a step further with Bluetooth peripherals or a Thunderbolt hub, but I didn't want too many pieces to the puzzle.
Beyond raw performance, I found the decoupled setup's user experience superior. I can tuck the mini PC out of sight and eliminate my HP Pavilion's inherent lap-warming tendencies too, creating a quieter and more comfortable work environment for extended stints.
The trade-offs
It's not all sunshine and giant screens
Despite its many advantages, this 100-inch laptop replacement has obvious limitations, of which only some affect me. First, you cannot use this system on a train, in a coffee shop, or during a layover at the airport lounge. It is a destination-based workstation. Its utility begins once you have a stationary space to work. For anyone who depends on the flow of working anywhere, at any time, this replacement setup is a non-starter. However, I prefer settling in to work than working in transit, so I don't view this as a limitation.
This setup is also entirely dependent on having a suitable projection surface—a large, clear, light-colored wall—which, while common in hotel rooms, is never guaranteed. Another tradeoff is the complexity induced by the multi-component setup. Instead of a unitary laptop and its charger, I must additionally carry an HDMI cable, keyboard, mouse, mini PC, and projector remote. The weight and volume both vastly exceed a bulky gaming laptop, and setup takes a moment longer than hitting the power button on a notebook. I'm just using what's on hand, but if I went out to buy the required bits, I'd get a pico projector. Down the road, I'm also looking for ways to connect Bluetooth peripherals to the projector and leverage its Android OS for my mostly web-based work.
Finally, there's the cost concern, and I'll be blunt — this option is pricier than an equivalent laptop, and doesn't make sense for everyone. You pay a compactness tax on the projector, mini PC, and power supply. It adds up quickly, but the experience is worth more than the sum of its parts to only a handful, myself included. Those intrigued by the concept but deterred by the price, could scale things down a notch. One could opt for a cheaper, dimmer pico-projector and a lower-specification mini PC. However, this introduces its own compromises in performance, image quality, and brightness, making the trade-offs harsher.
It's not for everyone
Ultimately, this modular approach is a compelling alternative for a certain type of traveler. This is fantastic if you prefer quiet stay-cations, or your work takes you to hotels for a few days when you'd value a large screen and decent performance over the ability to work from anywhere at a moment's notice with a laptop. For me, this redefined the idea of a travel PC by prioritizing the in-room experience, offering a massive, comfortable display and serious power in a package that's surprisingly portable. To me, this was a no-compromise workspace that feels less like a temporary setup and more like a home office away from home. I'm already looking forward to my next opportunity to use this setup.
